4.5 stars. Vi and Penelope have certainly figured out the magic combination of co-writing! They've given us another incredible book with all of the essential elements that go into making the perfect romance story. 
 Right off the bat we're drawn into the obvious chemistry that Carter and Kendall have. The lifestyle that Kendall is afforded is one that most people only dream of, having the financial ability to fly somewhere at the drop of a hat, and pilot Carter is living quite the life himself, getting to fly people all over the world to romantic and exotic locations. He has certainly been living the playboy pilot lifestyle, flight attendants galore, propositioning him at every turn, a never ending supply of willing participants who want a piece of the gorgeous pilot. 
 Vi and Penelope always create an engaging story that keeps me glued to the pages to see what's going to happen between the couples. How steamy will the sex be between them, what kind of adventures are they going to embark upon? Will the baggage from their pasts, and there's always some, get in the way of the characters forging a future together? 
 I was drawn to Carter right away. Yes, he was a typical manwhore and it seemed unavoidable that the women from his past would cause some type of drama throughout, and we got plenty of that. I actually felt sorry for Kendall for having to be subjected to so much of it. But I guess there was really no way around that since Carter seemed to have slept with every willing flight attendant out there. I will admit that part did make me want to slap him upside his head and yell the proverbial saying, "Don't shit where you eat!" 
 Kendall was a little harder for me to form a connection to. I liked her a lot on a superficial level, thoroughly enjoying the adventure she was going on with Carter. But when it got down to the nitty gritty of the story and what was going on with her, I felt a disconnect during this part, perhaps because when the climax of the story happens, it suddenly jumps forward 11 months and we find out what happens after the fact, instead of living through it with Carter and Kendall. I felt like I was right alongside these two for the whole story, and then suddenly it was like they got in a cab and took off without me, and I had to take the next one to catch up with them. 
 I loved the scene in the airport when Carter happens to run into one of Vi and Penelope's previous, very much loved characters. I'm really enjoying how their other characters are making little cameos in each subsequent book, that is awesome!! 
 Another great story from Penelope and Vi!! I can't wait to see what they come up with next!!

 Drew Jagger

 Emerie Rose

***NO SPOILERS*** 
 Let me begin by saying I had no high expectations for this book just because it was written by JK Rowling. The only assumption I made before reading it was that the summary sounded like it would be a light-hearted, funny observance of silly small town life. I could not have been more wrong about that - this book delves into the dark, tragic side of small town existence. 
 For me, the book is really divided into 2 distinct halves. The first half got three stars because it was well-written, but didn't really keep my attention. She introduces a huge cast of couples and characters very quickly and it's kind of hard to keep them straight until you are further into the book. In addition, many of the characters (most) are just not that likeable. This part of the book really centered on character development and setting the stage for the second half. 
 But half way through the book, you really understood the characters' motives and the plot got more complicated. I actually stayed up until 1:00 a.m. to finish - I haven't done that with a book since Harry Potter and the Deathly Hollows. Growing up in a small town, I recognized so many of these characters as real people and found it very interesting that their struggles and viewpoints are universal. You have the small-minded pompous constituent, the abusive poser, the angry self-righteous one, the clueless shallow one. 
 In the end, the characters are in two distinct groups - adults and teenagers. Although all are tragically flawed, I felt the teenage set won the day as the quiet heroes of the story. 
 I think this book will stay with me for a while - 4 stars.

reference_books.title: Slade House
reference_books.review_text: I'm not a horror fan, but I loved this. I liked it better than Bone Clocks, actually. Fast read, especially for Mitchell.

reference_books.title: The Infinite Sea (The 5th Wave, #2)
reference_books.review_text: I love this series! Very well done, the second book might be even better than the first. I love that it isn't sappy, and in fact took a really different turn from Book 1. Note to self: read the first 2 books again before reading #3. I was a little lost early on, trying to remember what happened.

book_a.title: The Good Thief
book_a.user_review: Not a badly written book - I just thought it was kind of boring.

sample_reviews.review_text: One of the more exhilirating reads of my lifetime! I REALLY enjoyed this novel and was surprised by how much I cared for the protagonist orphan boy. The situations he found himself in were a little unbelievable, but this is an excellent story.

Took me a little while to really get into the book, but all audiobooks seem to take me awhile. The reader was okay, not the best I've heard. I liked the characters and the pacing, and it definitely sucked me in enough to make it through to the end.

I had a lot of issues with the intent of several scenes in this book. There were scenes inserted that felt like the direct result of an editor telling the author the story line was dragging. Also, I didn't quite buy the relationships between major characters. I especially didn't understand Ren and Dolly's commitment to each other; Benjamin/Harelip; Tom/the twins. None of it made sense to me and even when I told myself to just ride the wave; it still bothered me. I also feel, since you asked, that a lot of the characters were quirky for quirky's sake; not for any real reason (SPOILER: Why in gravy was the dwarf living on the roof?). There were very nice moments, of course. Mrs. Sands was a well written character. Ren, the title character, also fully developed and believable. 
 For a more endearing and a more believable QuirkFest, try The Little Giant of Aberdeen County or Geek Love, IMHO.
Enjoyable read, but it seemed to end really quickly - as if all the loose ends needed to be tied up on a deadline.

This Dickensian adventure story of an orphan boy who makes good by teaming up with a pair of grave robbers is a bit bleak in the telling, but more than makes up for it in the happily-ever-after ending (which is still realistic). Colorful characters enliven the 18th century setting and help the small bedraggled hero make his way in a confusing adult world. Accessible prose and a good eye for historical detail made the pages fly!

I enjoyed almost everything about this book. As I've said so, so many times in the past, I really do lose it for a book with gaslights and stolen horses. I can't get enough. 
 While Ren's not the most dynamic character of the 21st century, he's an engaging narrator. Benjamin, however, is more two-dimensional, and the plot twists sometimes skewed a little contrived. (I'm thinking of REN, for one.) 
 Some of the details and characterizations seemed bizarre for bizarreness' sake (Why the "hat boys?" Why not? And what about the harelip? And the dwarf and his toys?), which threw me out of the realm of the book. It was sort of a magical realism effort, and I give Ms. Tinti a lot of credit for creativity and writing, but every now and again the plot spun out of her control.

Phillip Pullman without the ethics. Harry Potter without the charm. Roald Dahl without the humor. So what do you have? A series of loosely connected scenes filled with brutality, drugs, alcoholism, grave-robbing, and more brutality. The only character I cared for (including 12-year old Ren who had the personality of a paper doll) was the horse. And she came to a (predictably) brutal end. A truly awful book, written for 10 year olds corrupted by a steady dose of television. Describing it as "gothic" and "spooky" doesn't begin to cover the underlying cynicism.
I listened tot he audio book and that is the only reason I finished it - very strange and gruesome book.
I missed something with this book...didn't like any of the characters and didn't get the premise

From the description and the many positive reviews, I expected a Dickensian-style young adult novel. It started out interestingly enough, with the protagonist being an 11 year old orphan who is missing his left hand. He has no idea who he is or where he came from, he just wants to be adopted and have a family of his own. So far, so good. One day a strange man comes to the orphanage and, claiming to be the boy's long-lost brother, takes him away. From there, things take an almost cartoonishly dark and violent turn. The rest of the book is filled with thieves, grave robbers, murderers, and "colorful" characters who seem to have no reason to be part of the story. Every character is two-dimensional, with no explanation for how they got to be the way they are and do the things they do. It's not even clear what time period this is supposed to be. The setting is somewhere in New England, but the boss bad man is the only one who speaks with a (phonetically written) New England accent. I guess that was supposed to make him seem extra-psycho, but it just made it awkward to read.

book_b.title: Big Little Lies
book_b.user_review: 3.5 stars, but I rounded up. I was a little annoyed with the first half of the book - it seemed like a rehash of what Moriarty does (catty school moms) but without making you care much about the characters. But the second half was a subtle change; everything became more serious, and it pulled you in. I love that Moriarty addresses domestic violence, even though the topic was kind of handled at a surface level. The ending was something I didn't see coming, I loved it.

sample_reviews.review_text: Read this for the second time - enjoyed it even more - possibly because I am currently watching the series on tv. Love Liane's books.

I devoured this book. Liane Moriarty is a masterful writer at the top of her game. I was blown away by the characters, the twists and turns of the plot, and the way the structure of the story kept me turning the pages. Satisfying ending, too. Perfect, perfect, perfect book. Really first rate.
5 stars for this book because I COULD NOT put it down! Such a fun read.
This is such a great, quick read! (I just had a baby and needed something that was easy to process; this fit the bill.) It was funny, interesting and highly enjoyable!

This started off a little slow. But soon I started to care about the characters and the book just flew by. I loved the way it built up to the ending. It was exciting. So much better than the Husbands Secret.
Loved!
Fantastic book!!!
This felt very similar to her other book at first although it grew on me about 1/2 way through.
I loved this book! I definitely recommend it and couldn't put it down!

Loved this book more than the Husband's Secret. I cannot wait to see it brought to life by actors and actresses in the near future, as this book was really character oriented. Such interesting characters that I built in my mind through the author's words! Fun read.

reference_books.title: The Corrections
reference_books.review_text: Franzen is without a doubt a genius and he loves words. He uses words to take you into the heart and soul of his characters. I do not really enjoy reading his novels but once I start a book, I just have to finish it. I find his work very dark and sad. His characters can not find happiness, tho they try and try. They are bright people but are judgmental, competitive, mean, angry and liars. I am glad that I have read The Corrections and Freedom, but will probably not read anything else by him. I choose to be happy during my short time here on earth, so why am I reading about people who don't.

reference_books.title: Zeitoun
reference_books.review_text:
I wanted more information about the storm and how everyone reacted to it. More about the prison and less about Zeitoun's family. But I know that FEMA could be impossible to really understand let alone the Homeland Security institution. 
 What I loved the most was the ending. Zeitoun's is a fighter and has great pride in his country, his company , his family and most importantly- a huge forgiving heart.

reference_books.title: The Interestings
reference_books.review_text: Very tedious-- skipped a lot.

reference_books.title: The Storied Life of A.J. Fikry
reference_books.review_text: Loved every word.

reference_books.title: The Things They Carried
reference_books.review_text:
You hold your breath - your heart breaks- you feel sick- angry- how did this war happen? Tim O'Brien's story is shockingly real. It is a beautiful hymn to the men he knew, loved and lost. 
 "...and when I take a high leap into the dark and come down thirty years later, I realize it is as Tim trying to save Timmy's life with a story."

book_a.title: A Widow for One Year
book_a.user_review: Wonderful unconventional love story.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Grade: F 
 Hated this book. I only read the first section. After hearing the fellow book clubbers thoughts on the novel I was glad I didn't bother to finish it!

I think this book is way too long, and although has some interesting plots, I felt it lacked something. In my opinion the worst thing about this book was the disapointing way in which all the promising stories ended. 
 Irving writes fantastically, he creates conflicts and situations that are intriguing and fascinating and just when he had all myattention he just solves the situation in the most unsatisfying way possible (killing characters, solving misteries way too easily, etc) 
 I fealt like I was cheated, too many pages, not enough emotion.

I think there is a waste of a real talent in all this effort to achieve an erotic meaningless prolonged tale. Sex in this novel is just like playing hockey with a teenage impatience to play with the same team for long.Bored me to death and wasted my time!
interesting
I really disliked all of the characters in this book.

This is one of those 537-page books that, after you've read about 100 pages, you realize you've pretty much seen what the author's handing out and you don't care for it. This is a drag because there is so much more of it to go and only some misguided impulse to finish what you've started goads you stubbornly onward. 
 What's not to like? Well, here's some: 
 At times Irving writes with the grace of a ballet dancer and at others he lumbers along like a blindfolded football player looking for an exit. The word 'clumsy' comes to mind. 
 I found some of the things his characters said, and many of their actions, unlikely and unbelievable. (His main character chooses to build her workroom in the room where her father committed suicide after a fight with her. She can still smell carbon monoxide fumes (his chosen exit strategy) from the cars below. How...atmospheric. This is a good place to write a novel?) 
 The characters' interactions and lives also seem unreal. The knotted combinations of who is in love or having sex with whom, the main character finding lasting love after a couple of weeks of being with a guy after her continual failures with other men...just no, okay? 
 Also objectionable: the 'comic' parts that deteriorate into vaudeville slapstick...specifically the jilted adulteress gunning for her seducer with her car. 
 One thing that was interesting was a convoluted device that had characters commenting and reflecting on how much or little novel writing contains autobiographical vs. imaginative content. At times this was like looking in a mirror and seeing yourself holding a mirror and looking back. 
 Even so, I will unhesitatingly jilt John himself. I hope he doesn't have a Lincoln!
Enjoyable sections interspersed by a preponderance of flash-aheads, flash-backs, and reiterations.

It pains me to give a book written by Irving only one star, but I felt the subject matter was distasteful and none of the characters were likable. Oh, I empathized and sympathized and wanted to like them, but alas, i just could not make the leap. Furthermore, and for this I apologize, but it cannot be helped, I cannot but hold up the bar of A Prayer for Owen Meany to his other works. That was the first of his that I had read and by far one of my favorite books read to date so that just added to the disappointment. Lastly, I have read this book before. I knew the story. I had utterly forgotten every last bit of it until I was reading each portion of it, "Ah yes. This DOES happen. Oh! I knew that was what happened, so then I know what's coming next." That I have read this and couldn't not remember having had read it until I came upon each "new" chapter, cannot be entirely my fault as a reader, but a flaw in the story and the writing. I think it was my distaste for the subjects and the situations within the novel that I must have put the whole thing out of my mind. I will give him credit for his "Dickensian scope" that was never the problem and as always, kudos to Irving for that. This book was just not meant for me.

This was my first John Irving book, and what a book it was. Where even to begin? 
 From the very first pages, I knew I liked it. A promise that the 16 year old loving a depressed mother would 30+ years later fall in love with her daughter- I couldn't wait for the story to unfold. Alas, I did much of that; wait. 
 The story goes on, and on, and on, but one thing I (think I) like about John Irving is that his writing is so easy to read that you start not to notice that you're reading (you feel me??). It's plain and simple. You're following along, and everything is flowing. There's no impatience, only enjoyment. And I guess that is what good writing is. 
 Did he talk about breasts a lot? Yeah. Was he describing the shape of women's nipples, and men's shlongs? Yeah. But did I pick it up every time looking forward to reading more? Yeah.
I picked this up because I liked the movie A Door in the Floor, and I ended up hating it.

book_b.title: All the Ugly and Wonderful Things
book_b.user_review: Um ..not my kind of story. For me, it was very hard to read. But, the author does a fine job of introducing you to a way of life that you might not know--very harsh and sad.

sample_reviews.review_text: This book is heavy, and covers a whole lot of tough subject matter, but the writing was simply fantastic. The style of story telling leaves you to make your own decisions about the characters and the tough subject matter (i.e. pedophilia) without feeling as though the author is cramming her opinions into a fictional story. My feelings and opinions didn't much matter either, because the story was so compelling that I couldn't put the book down until I had finished reading it.
Not all books are about pleasant or PC things. This is one of them. Beautiful, disturbing, and haunting.

Omerzitel'no, gadko, otvratitel'no. Ia kak budto izvalialas' v griazi. Kniga ogromnaia, i ia vse vremia pytalas' vynyrnut' i podyshat' chistym vozdukhom, no mne snova prikhodilos' v nee pogruzhat'sia. 
 Nesmotria na to, chto eta kniga - samoe otvratitel'noe, chto ia kogda-libo chitala, stil', osobennosti i iazyk avtora ochen' interesny. Oni napomnili moi liubimye knigi, takie kak: Making Faces by Amy Harmon i The Strange and Beautiful Sorrows of Ava Lavender by Leslye Walton. Povestvovanie vedetsia ot pervogo litsa, no glavy mogut byt' ot litsa kogo ugodno (prichem ot litsa geroev ne tak uzh chasto), chut' li ni mimo prokhodiashchikh liudei: kuziny Veivi, podrugi iz kolledzha, sherifa, malen'kogo brata geroin i t.d. Istoriia nachinaetsia s rannego detstva geroini, tak skazat', izdaleka. Iazyk neplokhoi, avtor pishet khorosho, i ia mogu poniat', pochemu kniga poluchila nagradu ot Goodreads, no siuzhet nastol'ko omerzitelen, protiven i nevynosimo zatianut, chto ia ne smogla po dostoinstvu otsenit' eto proizvedenie. 
 Sobytiia razvivaiutsia v 70-80-ykh gg XXv. v Oklakhome. 
 Vot i khotelos' by otnestis' k personazham s ponimaniem, pozhalet' ikh, no ne mogu. Prosto ne mogu sebia zastavit'. Chto on, chto ona... chto okruzhaiushchie... Ia ni za chto by ne zakhotela, chtoby eti liudi okazalis' so mnoi riadom. Navernoe, nuzhno otdat' avtoru dolzhnoe: ona dostatochno khorosho propisala personazhei, chtoby vyzvat' u menia takuiu nenavist'. No dlia menia seichas eto ochen' slozhno. 
 Personazhei million, u vsekh svoia istoriia, korotko (ili ne korotko) rasskazannaia nam avtorom. I ia takoe obychno ochen' liubliu, no tochno ne v etom sluchae. 
 Ia daleko ne khanzha, vot uzh tochno, no dazhe mne eto vse bylo nastol'ko protivno... Avtor pokazyvaet nedalekimi idiotami okruzhaiushchikh geroev, kotorye ne ponimaiut i vystupaiut protiv otnoshenii 13-letnei devochki i 25-letnego ogromnogo baikera. I da, eti okruzhaiushchie i menia vyvodili iz sebia (tam uzh oni chereschur lezli ne v svoe delo), no ia tozhe ne mogu etogo poniat'. Ia ne veriu v <<liubov'>> s pervogo vzgliada (20-letnego parnia v 8-letniuiu devochku), o kotoroi vsiu knigu taldychit avtor. S chego by vdrug? My vidim vsiu ikh istoriiu, i ona deistvitel'no gadkaia. Bednaia devochka, kotoroi i tak v zhizni ne povezlo, eshche i takogo parnia poluchila. Da, soglasna, on ei mnogo pomogal, oberegal, no odnovremenno i razvrashchal (delaia vid, chto eto ne tak, no eto vran'e, on prosto uspokaival svoiu sovest', on nikak ee ne ostanavlival). 
 Vozmozhno, mne ochen' povezlo v zhizni s sem'ei (ne vozmozhno, a sovershenno tochno), i ia prosto ne mogu iz-za togo, chto ne videla nichego podobnogo v real'nosti, poniat' geroev... nu, togda prosto skazhu: eta kniga opredelenno ne dlia menia. Vse eti podrobnye opisaniia seksa, kak ona s nog do golovy byla v ego sperme, bezzastenchivo rasskazannye trinadtsatiletnei devochkoi, sovershenno tochno ne dlia menia. Nichego ne imeiu protiv opisaniia seksa v knigakh, no ne v etom sluchae. 
 Ia videla sotni takikh <<porno>>-knig o baikerakh, zapadavshikh na dochek bossa, no ia nikogda ikh ne chitala, schitaia musorom. Gliadia na reiting i priznanie etoi knigi na Goodreads, ia dumala, ona o chem-to drugom. Vozmozhno, tak i est', potomu chto pisat', kak ia uzhe govorila, avtor umeet bessporno, no siuzhet... Br... Dlia menia odnoi iz samykh bol'shikh zagadok v mire stal reiting etoi knigi na Goodreads. Ona ogromnaia, i ia ele ee dochitala, i prazdnovala neskol'ko chasov, kogda ona konchilas'. 
 Bol'she vsego menia razozlilo to, chto khot' geroi i dumal o tom, chto vse, chto on tvorit s trinadtsatiletnei devochkoi kak by nepravil'no, avtor polnost'iu opravdyvala vse ego postupki <<liubov'iu>>. A vse neodobrenie i nakazanie, kotoroe prishlos' ponesti geroiu, ob'iasnila nedalekost'iu okruzhaiushchikh, tem, chto oni ne znali, chto on ee po-nastoiashchemu liubit. Nu, ia vot vrode kak <<znala>>, no vse ravno ne poniala. 
 V obshchem, etakaia ocherednaia istoriia <<Lolity>>, no Nabokov khotia by ne opravdyval geroev i ne ustroil im kheppi-end>>.
Beautifully written, heartbreaking as well as hopeful. At times I had to stop and read something light and fluffy but I'm glad I stuck with it.

Let me start by saying this book is very well written. I found myself unable to put it down. The subject matter was pretty dark and you felt invested in the characters. About half way through the book it took a turn for me that I was not able to forgive. 
 ****Spoilers**** 
 No matter what this book tries to say about Wavy, 13 year olds are not mature enough to have that kind of relationship. I knew this was where the book was headed but I wished they would have made her older when their relationship shifted to more sexual. I am no prude but this was too much for me.

I'm sorry, but is there some kind of club that I'm not a part of? I really, really, really don't understand this book. I don't understand the raving reviews, I don't understand the characters, I don't understand the plot, even. Am I just hating it because I don't understand it? Maybe, maybe not. Maybe this book sucks. 
 The book started off with potentials, of course. Then it just became all mumble jumble. From the beginning, I felt like the author was building it up so much and couldn't follow through. Like she had this grand idea that got abruptly interrupted, but she didn't know how to make it better so she just left it. There was no character development whatsoever. And I know, I know, people keeps saying you have to have "an open mind" to read this book, and so I prepared myself. I still came out of it unfulfilled and disappointed. 
 I'm so sad, truly. Just because a book is controversial doesn't mean it should automatically get great reviews or win all these awards. I guess it's true that tragic is the new success nowadays.

I was considering giving this book three stars, but it left me with a sick feeling in my stomach as I closed it. There was a lot to like about this book; the best part for me was the writing, which was just beautiful, even when it was describing horrific things. I felt that the book took a long time to get going plot-wise, but once it did, I couldn't put it down. 
 As a writer, I don't want to try to tell other writers how to end their books; but the ending of this book just doesn't sit well with me. I kept thinking the author would turn it around at the last second and give Wavy the ending I believe she deserved. Instead, Bryn Greenwood chose to end her novel by having the main character end up in a "happily ever after" situation with a pedophile who looked at her/treated her sexually from the age of eight . This book still gets two stars from me because the writing was great and I mostly enjoyed reading it; but I feel that Bryn Greenwood had the chance to condemn some extremely disturbing behavior, and instead she chose to reward and romanticize that behavior.

This is a highly controversial book and I look at it from two angles: a reader and a mother. As a reader, I love the story. It is sad and profound and moving. As a mother, I find the story highly disturbing. It is all too realistic for some kids. Part of the reason that I loved this book so much is how much is made me think. It raises so many questions.

4.5 stars 
 This was touted as a "meth lab romance" when it was chosen as an August BOTM pick, and that's really what drew me in- 
 Wavy is a young girl living with two abusive, good for nothing, drug addicted parents. She is often neglected and left to her own devices, and is befriended by an adult man Kellen, who works as a drug runner for Wavy's father. 
 Wavy is very introverted, to the point where she doesn't even talk. She is obviously a very intelligent girl, but people don't know what to make of her. Over the years, as Kellen becomes her rock and the one person she knows she can rely on, Wavy slowly emerges from herself and finds her footing in the world. 
 Meanwhile, you still have the very seedy setting of a trailer compound where everyone fawns over Wavy's father. No one seems at all fazed that Kellen is spending such an inordinate amount of time with a minor child, driving her around on his motorcycle and showing up at her house at all hours. It sounds creepy as hell I'm sure, and yet I found myself rooting for Wavy and Kellen. 
 All the Ugly and Wonderful Things spans over ten years, starting when Wavy was 8. {SPOILERS} And as time wore on and Wavy's relationship with Kellen turned sexual, it almost seemed natural. And their relationship certainly didn't feel sinister or wrong. And I began to wonder wtf was wrong with me that I wasn't totally disgusted by their relationship. 
 I read some other reviews and chatter about this book as I finished it because I wanted to know whether I was alone in my feelings or not and I was relieved to see that I wasn't. That was part of the reason I loved this book. It was one of those books that turned all my preconceived notions on their head and made me question how I truly felt. And it showed me that maybe everything isn't as black and white as it appears. And I am still uncomfortable with how I feel.

Mmm... ?Que decir? 
 Tenia mucho tiempo sin leer un libro de literatura juvenil, ninguno me atrapaba lo suficiente y debo admitir que este logro que me lo leyera de tiron. La tematica me intrigaba, pense que se aproximaria a una Lolita moderna. No, no lo hizo. 
 Le doy tres estrellas porque no estuvo ni muy bien ni tan mal. Me gusto la historia, pero le falto mucho. Tenia demasiados elementos y la autora queriendo anadir tantas cosas se olvido de desarrollarlas como se merecian, creo que menos cosas con mas empeno hubiera funcionado mejor. El libro no me rompio el corazon, no me hizo replantearme mi vida, si logro que me sintiera incomoda en algunas escenas, y eso estuvo bien, esa es la idea, que los libros te hagan sentir algo. 
 Creo que mi resena es un poco pesimista, y me gustaria escribir mas, pero no es un mal libro, es solo que "esta bien".

reference_books.title: The Collector
reference_books.review_text:
There are much better abduction books out there than The Collector by John Fowles. As a public service, I would like to draw your attention to Room by Emma Donoghue, which is about a mother who gives birth to her son in a basement, where she'd been abducted and forcefully detained for the past five years. Compared to this book, Room is a lot more moving story from beginning to the end. 
 With The Collector, I was hoping to get the abductor's perspective on things, which I didn't get in Donoghue's work -- what goes through an abductor's mind? What makes him do it? How does he rationalise it? What kind of preparations does he make before he commits the crime? Unfortunately, the predators are oftentimes more fascinating than the prey, and that was part of the reason why I decided to pick this up. 
 The first third of the book is promising. Told from the abductor's point of view, we get to know this sexually inept, character-free antagonists who kidnaps the protagonists because she's, well, beautiful. You get to see his thought process before the crime, and how strange he is to not sexually assault her throughout the book -- a very rare thing in such cases. 
 Then, the book changes perspective to Miranda, the abductee's. Unfortunately, this is also the point when the book takes a turn for the worse. Told from Miranda's point of view, the second act of the story is a series of diary entries -- cliched, I know. As a reader, you then have to sit through every single event that has already been described before in a completely new perspective. Plus, Miranda also goes to great (unnecessary) lengths to talk about her life prior to the kidnap, especially her love/crush for a man named GP -- likely the most boring part of the book. I found it difficult to draw a line between the GP stuff and the kidnap at hand. It felt disjointed and detached, completely isolated from the rest of the narrative. 
 By the time the story shifted back to the antagonist's point of view, I had already lost interest. Worse, I was no longer rooting for Miranda to survive. She comes across as being naive and helpless, and revealing her past only serves to annoy me more. When it is revealed that she passes away from an illness, I couldn't care less -- just like I cannot care less about this book.

reference_books.title: A Night in the Lonesome October
reference_books.review_text:
Do not be fooled by the positive ratings on Goodreads or the enticing synopsis you will find of this book online. A Night in the Lonesome October is likely one of the most disappointing books that I have read this year. What I dislike most about this book is the fact that you have a great cast of literary characters, from Jack the Ripper and Dracula to the Wolfman and Doctor Frankenstein, all coming together to perform a ritual that either closes a portal that lets in Lovecraft's Elder Gods or opens it. The fate of the world hangs in the balance between these folks. Yet, you limit the perspectives to their animal companions, which have zero characters and zero personality. Big events, like murders and betrayal, happen off the page, so the animals only learn about them after the fact. 
 What is worse is that the actual plot of the book is only explained at 83% of the book. 83%! That's like reading 83% of The Lord of the Rings, then finding out that Frodo's task is to get the One Ring to Mount Doom to destroy it. 
 I have read better works from Roger Zelazny. Far better works. This is not it.

reference_books.title: The Sparrow (The Sparrow, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
The scientists are idiots, and here are the reasons why: 
 1. They went in search of an alien civilisation by -- literally -- flying in the general direction of Alpha Centauri. They figured out the exact location along the way. 
 2. They arrived at the alien planet, THEN attempted to figure out where to land their spacecraft. Imagine if NASA had done that for the moon landing in the 1960s. 
 3. They tested the edibility of alien vegetation and wildlife by EATING said alien vegetation and wildlife. 
 4. When someone died from the alien diet, our scientists couldn't quite figure out why. 
 5. They weren't able to return to their spaceship in orbit because someone literally used up the fuel in the lander just to show off to the leader of the team. 
 6. They didn't have a clue what to do upon meeting the aliens for the very first time. No SOPs, nothing. 
 7. They emerged out of the lander for the very first time, on an alien planet, without spacesuits. 
 8. They disregarded the possibility of contaminating the aliens with pathogens. 
 9. They disregarded the possibility of being INFECTED by alien pathogens. 
 10. They spent six weeks on an alien planet before one of them said, hey, maybe we should start planting our own food -- YOU THINK? 
 11. They plant human food on an alien planet and disregarded the possibility of destroying the local ecosystem. 
 12. They had no way to maintain radio contact with Earth, and shrugged it off because "everyone they loved was on the planet with them". 
 Most of the characters end up dead by the hands of the locals. This is not a spoiler. 
 They deserved to die, anyway. God damn idiots, all of them. 
 These 'scientists' are the dumbest characters in all of science fiction literature.

reference_books.title: The Sacred Lies of Minnow Bly
reference_books.review_text:
2.5, really. 
 The Sacred Lies of Minnow Bly is by no means a bad book, but I think there is less to this book than what the author wants us to believe. The breezy style of writing makes this an easy and enjoyable read for the most part, but it is not quite enough to conceal the fact that it just doesn't have a whole lot going for it. 
 This story, about a girl who grew up in a modern-day cult, reminds me somewhat of One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest and Room somehow. The former, because one story is focused on the protagonist's experience in a juvenile prison; the latter, because the protagonist, after being rescued from the cult, has to erase years of brainwashing under the 'Prophet' and relearn the world. 
 However, this book is not as good as either of the above examples. The result is a flashback narrative that is fairly interesting, but a present-day narrative that feels a lot like fluff. The characters you meet there are your cookie-cutter characters from, say, Orange is the New Black, but maybe without the humour. There is even a prisoner, convicted of murder, who teaches the protagonist about science and Carl Sagan. Not to say that such individuals do not exist, but just feels a little contrived. 
 Themes about captivity, religion and guilt do come up in the story, but it feels sometimes too on the nose. It feels like the author wanted to write a book about growing up in captivity, the dangers of religion and getting over guilt, then figured out a way to get there -- reverse engineering, basically. The result is a back-heavy narrative that feels lopsided. The final pages are filled with thematic takeaways, hammered over the head of the readers. Like I said, it's a little on the nose. 
 The central mystery is also highly predictable. Right from the get-go, you have about three suspects in mind. In fact, a detective eventually tells the protagonist that he had it figured out long before their interview in the prison even started. So the central conceit, the thing that keeps the readers guessing, is dampened quite a bit. 
 All of that aside, though, it is still a fairly readable book, though I will likely forget about the details three months down the road. A more accurate rating would be 2.5 -- just a passing grade, because I don't think it doesn't deserve any less or more.

reference_books.title: Authority (Southern Reach, #2)
reference_books.review_text:
The word "disappointment" doesn't begin to describe my feelings towards the second book in the Southern Reach Trilogy. In Annihilation, even though Area X was not forthcoming with the answers, but at least the pacing and mystery kept the plot moving at a good clip. I bought into what Jeff Vandermeer was selling and went into Authority with open arms, ready for answers and more of the same creeping atmosphere. 
 But NO. 
 During the final pages, I experienced severe physical reactions to reading this book -- and not in a good way either. Half the time, I was resisting the urge to toss the book against the nearest wall. It was hard work, and my palm was sweaty from the exertion. Every fabric of my body told me to stop reading the horrible book, but I have invested too much in the series to give up. I just had to slog through the pool of wet cement. I thought, hey, maybe this is the kind of book people refer to as a "slow burn". Maybe it will pick up at the halfway point. Besides, if it ends off with a bang, maybe it will be worth the ride, no matter how slow and bump it is. 
 But NO. 
 I'd have welcomed a bumpy ride, a drive out on rugged roads. At least it'd have proven to be more exciting than the sad slog that I've had to wade through. I have nothing against the fact that the focus was shifted to the Southern Reach rather than Area X. In fact, right from the get-go, several questions were already being answered, thanks to the fact that our protagonist here (named Control) approached Area X and Southern Reach with a fresh pair of eyes. He helped us ask the questions that we wanted to ask, and as the new director, some answers were certainly coming in. 
 Then the story took a turn for the worse into NOTHING-VILLE. Everything you really need to know about this book is concentrated in the first 50 pages of the book. There, you find out that Control was put there by his mother, who pulled some strings for him to be there; you find out that Grace, the assistant director, doesn't like the fact that Control is, for the lack of a better word, taking control; you find out that the psychiatrist from the previous book was, in fact, the former director of the organisation; you find out that three members of the previous expedition were recovered and brought in for questioning. THAT'S IT. The next 200 pages will tell you NOTHING NEW about Area X and Southern Reach. And forget about character development, because there will be NONE to speak of. Control is the same naive, jaded character at the end as he is at the beginning, and he spends half the book brooding about his role in the greater scheme of things. Area X is definitely an exciting and intriguing place, but Vandermeer decided that no, we should spend 200 pages of the book buried inside Control's thoughts. It's like going on a beach vacation, only to spend half the time in the hotel room because you hate the sun. WHAT'S THE POINT OF IT ALL? Control's not even a likeable character to begin with, and it is very hard to relate to someone who's so detached from everything. Every chapter involving him ends with questions -- questions for himself, questions about the world, questions about his mother, questions about the biologist -- SHUT UP. 
 There are no high points to this book and everything is flat. And Vandermeer thought it'd be a good idea to not follow a chronological order in the way he tells the story. He'd allude to something happening, move the plot forward, the flashback to tell what happened back there. It's sort of like running your truck into a deer on the highway, driving on for for the next half an hour, and then turning back just to look at the carcass. He also does this without warning, so all of a sudden, you are back in a previous scene, reading dialogue between two characters you do not give two shits about. 
 I enjoyed SOME bits of this book, especially the interrogation of the biologist. I wanted to hear her talk more, and at least that plot had some solid progress. As a reader, I could see her opening up to Control more and more, and even though she couldn't actually remember much from her days in Area X, it was fun to read her back and forth with Control. 
 But good things never last for long. 2/3 of the way through, the biologist is TAKEN AWAY, and Control is like, oh no, now I have to LIVE WITH MYSELF. Shut up, Control, you know what's worse than you living with yourself? US READERS BEING STUCK THERE WITH YOU. Control's a pinball in the greater scheme of things, trapped between the mysteries of Area X and his manipulative bosses at Central (including his MOM). So essentially, Control's story is really the story of a pinball, bouncing from one place to the next. 
 The only reason why I am reading the third book is because 1) I bought it 2) reviews seem to indicate that book three is a vast improvement 3) reviews seem to indicate that book three will have answers 4) reviews seem to indicate that, if you hated book 2, you'd love book 3. I am trusting the opinions of my peers here, because if the series continues to read like Authority, my brain is going to haemorrhage and die a slow, painful death. I would rather swallow a bag of bricks than to go through this steaming pile of horse shit ever again in my life. If book 3 turns out to be a pleasant surprise, that will definitely redeem the series to some level. But Authority is always going to be the thorn in the side, the Achilles' heel at the end of it all. It's just too bad, because Area X has so much going for it.

book_a.title: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (Harry Potter, #4)
book_a.user_review:
READING HARRY POTTER FOR THE FIRST TIME AS A 20-SOMETHING 
 The fourth entry in the Harry Potter universe is also the story's darkest one yet. Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (GoF) has everything you've come to expect of a Harry Potter book, but with a markedly sinister overtone that will appeal to lovers of the dark -- like me. 
 Right out of the gate, you know GoF is a different beast altogether. Instead of locking the readers to Harry's perspective, Rowling, for the first time, moved the story away from Harry's life and to a deep, dark corner of the story. The opening pages of GoF are delicious evil, with a infant-like Voldemort killing a helpless housekeeper with the Killing Curse. The entire sequence set the tone of the rest of the book, and it's a pity that the movie did not capture the same vibe. 
 As a fan of dark fantasy, I must say that it rubbed off on me a little when GoF came around. Many of my friends prefer the story line at Hogwarts without the "dark stuff". That is to say, they like the lessons, the rivalries, the Quidditch matches, the creatures, you name it. I, on the other hand, prefer the spine-tingling stuff, or anything that involves Voldemort and his minions. Say what you will about my official sorting on Pottermore (I'm in Ravenclaw), but there will always be a part of me, I suppose, that belongs to Slytherin. 
 However, that is not to say that I dislike Harry's lighter adventures. Rowling keeps the usual offerings interesting enough for people like me. And, again, her new characters continue to be intriguing, with Moody being the stand-out (even though, spoiler, he's not actually Moody throughout most of the book). 
 Now that I am at book four, it is easy to see that these Harry Potter books follow a trend. By that, I mean the books usually remain an enjoyable read for me until about 80% of the way through. After that, they either remain the same or they go to a whole new level. Just as how the Prisoner of Azkaban displayed its cleverness and wits only towards the end of the book, GoF came into itself only at the end when the story took a dark and gothic turn. Everything about Wormtail's sacrifice to Voldemort's resurrection was delicious for me as a reader. 
 Also, something about the length of GoF. This is the first time Rowling saw a need to expand her books. The first three books clocked in at about 200-300 pages, whereas this one went well over 600. You can feeling Rowling's attempts at spreading butter over too much bread right at the beginning before the Quidditch World Cup. In fact, I was a little bored with the introduction of a bunch of characters (who is Mr Roberts, again?) Nonetheless, I am happy to report that Rowling does eventually find her footing once the First Task was kicked off. 
 In a way, THIS is the true beginning of the Harry Potter universe, and everything before this is a skirmish. Voldemort has been a whisper in the winds in the first three books, but not anymore. This time, it's getting serious, and seriously personal. I cannot wait to see how it all unfolds.

sample_reviews.review_text: Another excellent book. The characters develop in maturity in leaps and bounds in this volume. There are several sub plots happening at the same time and J K Rowling weaves them brilliantly together. It amazes me the amount of planning that must have gone into the whole series before she sat down to write the first book. There are clues in the Goblet of Fire for the future stories that you will only notice if you know how the story ends. I'm glad I am rereading them all again. It's like going back to the series for the first time.
Good fun - I am now one book ahead of my 9 year old son. I predicted who was going to die very early on but the twist from a good character to a bad and back again to good was a genuine surprise.

Not one of my favourites, I don't really enjoy the inclusion of the Quiddich World Cup and some of the Triwizard Cup is boring. However, on the most part, it is still an enjoyable novel and a good pathway into the latter books.

The reason I decided to give it a 4/5 is because I feel that from the 4th book onwards, the Potter tales are a continuation into the next part...i.e. 1,2,3 had a definite beginning, middle and end...from part 4 onwards, there is a definite story line and the books are mesmerizing, but there are like a web- connected to each other and will not stand for too long if left alone

I was very surprised by this book, the level of detail is astounding and I had clearly forgotten a lot of it over the years. You can definitely tell these books are getting darker, more serious and it's clear even from this book how much Rowling planned about the ending of the series it's pure brilliance. 
 Harry has another tough year dealing with the triwizard tournament. His name was mysteriously placed into the goblet of fire without his knowing, and is forced to participate in three horrid tasks which could make him die. You can tell Harry is very determined throughout the tasks not because he wants to win or the glory he wants to stay alive. He is fighting for his life. He is very lazy when it comes to working on the clues for the task as he always leaves it till the last minute to work hard and worry about what he's doing. But of course as he is Harry Potter he pulls it off. For some of the book everyone is against him believing that he put his name in the goblet and got pasted the age restriction only wanting more fame and glory not willing to share it with anyone. 
 Even Ron his best friend doesn't believe him. There is a different side to Ron in this book. You can see he is very jealous of his brothers and Harry for getting attention and being noticed by everyone while he just falls to the sidelines. You can also see how he feels more about being poor and how Harry feels the need to hide and not brag about his money as he feels as if he would offend Ron. Ron is also very prejudice and racist towards giants and goblins as he believes they will eat humans and kill them where as Hermione and Harry can't understand what's wrong as they have grown up in the muggle world. At the end it just shows much Ron means to Harry when he is the on thing Harry would miss the most, it was adorable and so cute. I was so close to tears. Ron does prove he will do anything for Harry and helps him in his time of need. Ron is clearly jealous of Krum and probably doesn't understand his feelings for Hermione yet as he sees her as his best friend but was jealous! Nicely preparing for future books. 
 Hermione is a brilliant friend for Harry she believes him, helps him and most of all trusts him when everyone else doesn't. She is delighted by Victor Krum and takes the opportunity to be a teenage girl and have fun for a night. I really like how she had fun and didn't care what others thought of her and sure Ron got mad at her but she didn't let it ruin her time. Krum really liked Hermione as he even asked Harry about her which just showed that everything he did was for her as she is the thing he would miss most. 
 Sirius plays a more crucial role in this book than remembered as he gives Harry advice, meets him in Hogsmeade, writes him letter and is even at his bed side when he wakes up from the terrible ordeal. Sirius is taking the chance to be Harry's Godfather no matter how far away from him he is. I like how honest he is and doesn't hesitate to tell Harry the truth when others wouldn't because of his age. I just really like Sirius. 
 I really liked the part where the Weasley's came and surprised Harry in the champions tent that was so sweet as of course they're the closest thing to a family he has. It was perfect. I also really liked how we learnt more about Bill and Charlie in this book as we don't in the films. Bill working in Egypt for Gringotts and Charlie a dragon trainer in Romania. Percy is working for the ministry and is more stressed than ever now that Crouch has gone missing a d 'ill', the Weasley twins are working on a plan to start up their own business and everything seems to be going well for Ginny. 
 Mad-eye Moody returns to Hogwarts and is discovered to be Barty Crouch JR. and is the loyal servant Voldemort has been talking about. He helped Harry win and used this whole triwizard tournament to help voldemort return. It was very sneaky as a student was killed and he has no trouble in murdering his father or an innocent girl. It had a very complex story line as Barty Crouch's wife was dying and posed as Barty Crouch JR., Barty Crouch JR. was hidden under a cloak under the imperius curse his whole life and voldemort came to take back his servant. Barty Crouch sr was then put under the imperius and killed. So Barty JR. took on the role as Moody. 
 I love how Sirius stays with Harry to comfort and support him in his time of need when he retells all about the graveyard to Dumbledore. He is sent to gather more wizards for the next book, brilliant foreshadowing. 
 Cedric dies and Harry is of course beyond upset he feels like it's his fault, he should have won lived and got the money and glory he deserve. Voldemort has returned thanks to Wormtail the servant. Harry can't bare it and gives his prize winnings to Fred and George to help them start their shop as Barty was poor and gave them fake gold. I just love how much detail and thought has been put into the story and how it gives you hints for future books. Loved it.

This book was nerve gripping...seriously it had everything---> The action, The thrill, the suspense, the romance..I mean what else do you want!

 So 2 completely different schools with different headmasters heck different principles altogether... was a new detail added to my imagination of this magical world..The tournament and the manner of Harry's participation was entertaining and exhilarating... I was 12 or 13 and I seriously did not see Harry's participation coming..so then this part was a thrilling surprise..although had I read it now, I wouldn't be much surprised..it was definitely coming. 
 I did not care much about Cho Chang... Cedric Diggory i felt was less covered..I wanted to read and know about him more after I reached the part where he died to sympathise more with him.. 
 The tasks were an entertaining read...Hermione's appearance at the Yulle ball was what i wanted, Snape's negativity was always a pleasure, Moody was fun and I remember wanting to read more of the DADA classes...like every single lecture! 
 I mean every character introduced had a place in the story.. a part to play and shape the plot...every character was followable.. Basically you would never say-' Why did she even bring Dean/Seamus/Colin/Dennis/Skeeter/Stan/FAT LADY into the story!' NEVER!'
See here.

This was the last book of the series that I read as a child, I'm not sure why I stopped at it..I remember enjoying them so much. 
 I stayed up all night, just reading this book. Literally all night. I read and read and read, until I had finished it..i glanced up from the last page, and saw the sunrise. I panicked, threw the covers off my bed, and grabbed my alarm cock. I was quarter to seven in the morning, of a school day. 
 It dawned on me just how exhausted I was..I waited another half an hour to hear my mother wake up, then I went and told her what I'd done. I honestly expected her to be fuming..but she sort of..understood? And for the first time in my life, she let me have the day off school, and rang in saying I was ill. 
 - 
 I'll never forget that, I'll definitely never forget the feeling of just not being able to put a book down. That's the sort of phrase that is thrown around a lot in book reviews, but in the case of 'The Goblet Of Fire', it's 100% true. 
 I had no intention of staying up all night reading, but I just could not put it down. 
 This book (like almost all the others in the series) has made me laugh out loud in the middle of the night, it has made my chest swell with pride in the decisions that the characters make, it's made me feel sad, and happy, and curious, and all manners of other emotions. 
 - 
 I guess that at the end of the day though, it's fairly pointless reviewing Harry Potter books..if you read them with an open mind, there is simply no way that you won't enjoy them. 
 Everybody has been captivated by the incredible magic that's held within these pages, and there's no point in me trying to explain my adoration for these books any more, I am sure there are better literary critics out there that can voice their astonishment much better than I. 
 (This being the reason I haven't reviewed any of the others I've read.) 
 - 
 The first four books in the series are the ones I had read as a child, these last reads were just re-reads. 
 The next book (Order Of The Phoenix?) will be a completely new experience for me, and I cannot wait.

Originally published on my blog here in October 2001 and here in September 2011. 
 On first reading 
 The fourth Harry Potter novel, about as long as the other three put together, continues to match his increasing age by becoming more adult. A lot of The Goblet of Fire covers what is by now familiar territory; it begins with the summer holidays, and goes on to describe a school year, with elements such as the unpleasant Dursleys and Harry's fluctuating popularity at Hogwarts repeated from earlier novels. The main plot is about a competition between champions of the three schools of magic, in which Harry is entered even though below the age limit by an enemy who put his name in the magic implement which chooses the champion (the goblet of the title) in the name of a non-existent school, hoping to use the opportunity of the contest to harm Harry in the cause of dark wizard Voldemort. 
 There are some quite subtle differences, part of Harry's growing maturity. For example, his relationship with the Dursley's has been changing ever since he first went to Hogwarts, and now they are almost frightened of him and his friends. The changes which gained most publicity when the novel was first published, the handling of awakening sexuality and the additional seriousness brought by the death of a Hogwarts student, are more obvious, as is the increasing use of the techniques of the horror writer which begins with the introduction of the Dementors in Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban and which is continued in the chilling first chapter here. 
 Does the way that the series is developing make the fourth Harry Potter novel better than the first? The fact that it continues to grab the reader all the way through - to the extent that I stayed up all night reading it - is testimony to Rowlings' technical maturity. Like all the best children's books, the series has always included subtleties aimed at adult readers, but I suspect that younger fans are likely to find aspects of The Goblet of Fire off-putting. It certainly lacks some of the freshness of The Philosopher's Stone, and is far less humorous and exciting than the other novels. On balance, I probably enjoyed it less than its predecessors but admire it as an achievement, even if I wouldn't go so far as to say that it was as good a piece of fantasy as the Hugo award it has received implies. It is also not difficult to see why Rowling is taking longer than expected over the fifth novel, especially as she cannot really allow it to get any longer this time. 
 Re-reading in 2011 
 The fourth Harry Potter novel is something of a sudden change of gear for the series. It is much longer than the earlier novels, though shorter than those which follow. It is darker, starting with a killing and ending in an attack on Harry from which he barely escapes with his life as his companion is contemptuously killed with the command "Kill the spare" from Harry's enemy Lord Voldemort. And teenage sexuality starts to plan an important part in proceedings. 
 The story proper begins with the Quidditch World Cup, held in Britian over the summer holidays. The Weasleys have tickets to a match and invite Harry and Hermione to join them, but the even is ruined by an attack by Voldemort's death eaters on the Muggles at the campsite used for the crowds. The main plot of the novel is about the Triwizard Tournament, a most unusual competition between three champions, each representing one of the premier schools of magic in Europe. The tournament has been dormant for centuries because of the death toll, but it is revived at this moment for the sake of encouraging friendship among the schools; an extremely foolish thing to have done (sporting rivalry hardly ever leads to closer relationships between groups of opposing fans). The champions are chosen by a magical artefact, the eponymous Goblet, and Harry's name is chosen as an extra champion through a subterfuge, even though he is under the legal age to compete. This is effectively an attempt on his life, as the tasks the champions face would be pretty dangerous even for an adult wizard. . Naturally, few believe that Harry was innocent and didn't himself find a way to enter his name despite the charms in place to enforce the age limit, the assumption being that a celebrity will always embrace new opportunities for fame. Fame and its drawbacks are series themes, but this is the novel in which they are most prominent, probably as a reflection of some of Rowling's own experiences, particularly with the way that the press mis-reports Harry's activities, and the ethics-free zone which is reporter Rita Skeeter. 
 It seems to be a bit strange in terms of overall planning for the series to include the World Cup and the Triwizard Tournament in the same novel, but Rowling handles potential similarities quite well so that The Goblet of Fire does not appear to be too tediously sport related. 
 The longer story gives Rowling the space to be more expansive, which works quite well in the main. There are, however, a fair number of paragraphs, and even a couple of chapters, which could be cut completely without really being missed - The Weighing of the Wands, for example, adds minimally to the background, nothing constructive to the plot development, and nothing significant to the characterisation. Generally, Rowling uses the extra words to establish a stronger sense of atmosphere, which is one reason why The Goblet of Fire and the other later novels in the series come across as darker in tone. Before I re-read the novel, my memory suggested that the Quidditch World Cup was covered in a long-winded, hugely tedious manner over a hundred or so pages, but this isn't the case at all: the World Cup just takes a couple of chapters. 
 All in all, I feel that The Goblet of Fire is a below average entry for the series, but I am at something of a loss to explain why. There are holes in the plots of all of the books, but here it does in places seem particularly implausible. For example, the explanation given by Dumbledore about why Harry has to compete once his name has been drawn out of the goblet is rather unconvincing, since a magical artefact which has been so easily tricked into including his entry should not be difficult to trick again - particularly in a world with polyjuice and other tricks for hiding a wizard's identity. There would surely be some sort of safeguard built in, for example, if a chosen champion fell and broke their leg before the start of the first task, making them unable to compete through no fault of their own. More importantly, why was Dumbledore unable to detect changes in a friend of his who is being played by someone else magically transformed in appearance - it should be just about for Barty Crouch to play Moody in front of someone who knows him better. Moody himself advocated the use of questions with answers only known to the questioner and the person seeking to establish their identity as a test; why doesn't Dumbledore do that? Come to that, after the similar problem with Quirrell in Harry's first year, why aren't there charms around Hogwarts to make such an impersonation impossible? (The need to use a compromised teacher twice in the series suggests a certain poverty in Rowlings' imagination, too.) 
 I really quite liked this entry in the series a decade ago - my review was based on an all night reading session to finish the novel in one sitting. Other people also liked it: The Goblet of Fire was the only Harry Potter book to win a Hugo award. But on more careful re-reading ten years later, it doesn't really stand up so well.
