reference_books.title: Fahrenheit 451
reference_books.review_text: Bradbury explains in Zen and the Art of Writing that he was under a good deal of pressure when he cranked out his opus. He used pay typewriters, feeding in dimes that allowed him to compose. I'm sorry; I have a confession. I like that anecdote better than the novel. Surely his anticipation of iPods and wide-screen TV and the decline of reading should be appreciated, but the story just drags. Montag isn't a compelling character. Perhaps the passage of time has stolen some of the flavor from this oft-assigned chestnut.

reference_books.title: The Witch of Blackbird Pond
reference_books.review_text:
During my long-ago first year of teaching, we had a large stack of brand new Witch of Blackbird Ponds in the book room that we were supposed to teach seventh or eighth graders. Being new and unfamiliar with the text, I didn't get around to it for a while. But when I did, I realized why the stack was so large and pristine: it was too awful for even the most heinous middle school child. 
 Yep, it won a medal in 1958. But it just hasn't aged well. The pace is slow, the description laborious, and the conflict uninspired. With all of the excellent historical fiction out there for this age group, I hate to think that some will elect this title ONLY because it has that shinny sticker.

reference_books.title: Locke & Key, Vol. 6: Alpha & Omega
reference_books.review_text:
A satisfying conclusion to the five-volume set up. Little is left unanswered. Loose ends are tied up, although sometimes a bit too quickly. The series does a fine job looking at grief, good vs. evil, and the nature of growing into maturity. Read it all in one fast sitting, even though it is the longest book. If you haven't read the five prior titles, there's no point beginning here. 
 Now I am curious about Hill's work, graphic and otherwise.

book_a.title: The Dinner
book_a.user_review: The first third of this book took a real effort to get through. It appears to be social satire, a criticism of bourgeois civility and polite suburban-ism. Then, it descends into something else: an image of madness? There are twists and turns, surprises and shifts, but ultimately I didn't find this worth the effort. As a look into what parents will do for children, it is mildly interesting.

sample_reviews.review_text:
When I first read about this book I was excited to read it. It's a story about two couples who come together to discuss some Clockwork Orange level activities their sons engaged in recently. The two fathers are actually brothers - one an unemployed school teacher with anger management issues and the other an obnoxious celebrity politician poised to become the next prime Minister of Holland. The book has always been advertised as being disturbing, shocking, appalling .. basically just rock your socks off chilling to the core. Since its release, it's also been hyped up as being controversial. So it goes without saying that it was high on my To Read list. 
 Let me just say ... my socks were not rocked off. It start slow which works in the beginning. The narrator is the out of work brother and it's not too long before you realize there's something a bit off about him. But when it comes to this chill-you-to-the-bones crime the boys committed, you're halfway through the book before you get any clear idea of what's happened. To be fair, the crime is pretty heinous, so the book delivers in that regard. But the act itself isn't covered nearly as much as the narrator's feelings about the use of blank space when plating a meal in an upscale restaurant. Seriously - it's a theme he returns to, and dwells on, at least four different times in the book. 
 Simply put, The Dinner is a great premise poorly executed. The author spends too much time on everything except the plot and, as a result, readers end up feeling like a bored, fifth wheel at a dinner with four unpleasant people who are meant to come together to discuss a violent crime committed by their children but end up making it all about themselves instead. Maybe that's the point - maybe the author is trying to be clever and show how self-absorbed parents create sociopathic monsters and easily led thugs. But I feel I might be giving him too much credit with that. 
 23 Word Review: Two terrible couples raise horrible children, then get together to ignore the problems they created over an overpriced meal with sides of self-absorption.

Sick, twisted, ridiculously ambiguous. . . there is not a whole lot to like about this book. I cannot tell whether the author holds the viewpoint of his morally reprehensible characters or is mocking it. This book is about protecting children from vile mistakes they made, and avoiding consequences of extremely immoral actions. There is no lesson in this book, and I'm somewhat disgusted by it's contents. If someone feels they understand the deeper meaning of this book, please share, because I did not see it. SPOILER ALERT: Furthermore, the narrator and his son, and perhaps his wife as well, are psychologically ill, perhaps a combination of narcissism and bipolar, but the disorder is not revealed by the author. As someone who is studying to be a counselor, I would normally have empathy for someone like this, but the author does a great job of making sure I hate the characters. Perhaps that was his goal. For the number of great reviews this book got, what a disappointment and waste of my time.

I hated this book. I finished it hoping for something, anything, to happen at the end to make all the fuss worthwhile. And then nothing. It brings up some interesting moral dilemmas, but other than that, don't bother. Read Plato's Euthyphro if you need moral dilemma drama.
Wow! Great read! Many different layers! Great Book Club pick... So many topics to discuss!

** spoiler alert ** 
 I'm not sure if this book was poorly translated or just really bad in English. Then again, it could just be that I really hated this book. The writing is horribly stilted (which, as I said, could be a translation thing) and unrealistic. I didn't identify with any of the characters, in fact they just made me angry and hate them all by the end. I mostly stayed with the book to find out what the children (Michel and Rick, who are cousins) did. Luckily, you find out fast enough. They killed a homeless woman, which was apparently ok because she was in the way of the ATM machine and she smelled. Seriously, the fact that she smelled in pointed out multiple times and used as an excuse. The parents apparently feel that this wasn't that bad because A) she was homeless and it will blow over and B) she smelled and was in the way (Seriously, that's what Claire, Michel's mom, uses as an excuse for keeping quiet). Serge, Rick's father, seems to want to see justice for the woman, but only because the murder would effect his campaign. His idea to help this is to step down from the campaign, which his wife Babette is against for unclear reasons, and turn the boys in. Michel doesn't appear to feel bad about what he did, but according to Serge and Babette, Rick is suffering (this is repeated multiple times). How is this resolved? Claire, Michel's mother, attacks Serge with a wine glass so he can't resign. Then there's the issue that Michel and Rick are being blackmailed by Rick's adopted brother Beau because the morons recorded themselves killing the homeless woman and accosting another homeless man and Beau found them (because, shocker, Michel emailed the videos to Rick) and posted them on YouTube. How is this resolved? Well, Michel and Rick kill Beau. Claire even provides an alibi for Michel. Seriously, what the hell? Once again, the parents know and seem to be ok with this. Then there's the narrator, Paul. He just annoyed me with his constant whining about how his brother is a boor and an oaf and constantly reminding the reader that Claire is his wife. Then later you find out he's basically a sociopath who beat the shit out of his son's principle and his own brother at one point. Then there are the useless details the author drones about. There's the food, which is described in minute detail, the bathroom and how a man was peeing and what his junk looked like. Yeah. There are also some little side stories that seem to have nothing to do with the plot at all. In the end, no one seems to feel any guilt or remorse and I just felt disgusted with the characters.

Well, there is certainly a lot to talk about in this book: family relationships, pretentious fine dining, hazards of keeping secrets, the state of education, homeless people, casual violence, abortion, the death penalty...the list goes on. Unfortunately, not a bit of it is pleasant to think about and it certainly isn't pleasant to read about. I think I have reached my saturation point on books about awful people behaving in awful ways. 
 I knew this was a dark book when I picked it up. I've seen it compared to Gone Girl (a book I hated myself for loving) but this was more like a boring story about scary people. The kind of scary people that could be hiding in plain sight at the table next to you at a restaurant. I'm afraid that there are more people in the world like these creeps than I care to imagine but the events of today's world make it seem likely. 
 For pleasure reading, I can't recommend this. For a book to prompt discussion, it will be excellent.

I was only able to make it about 25% of the way through this book. Maybe it gets better later on. I don't know. I kept hearing that this book was the European Gone Girl, or even the European Defending Jacob. Maybe it becomes like that -- but the first quarter of it most definitely is as far from either of those books (the former of which I LOVED, the latter I at least enjoyed) as a book can get. Incredibly pretentious, hateful, and most of all BORING people eating dinner, with flashbacks of even more boring vacations and conversations. I know their sons did something (cuz that's the whole premise of the book), but I have no clue what, because it has not even been hinted at at this point (except that there's something on the one kid's phone about it). I can tolerate hateful protagonists, and kind of get a kick out of deceptive narrators (adds to the twists and turns). But I cannot tolerate boring. After realizing that I had zoned out and actually missed several pages -- due to the excessive boringness -- for the 5th or 6th time, I gave up and put the book down (and I never do that)
Permissive parenting meets situational ethics in this twisted story about a seriously messed up family.

Drippy and full of plot holes--not the "I'm having so much fun I don't care!" kind.The slow reveal of the nature of the narrator (through his own words) was nicely done and kept me reading, but the center couldn't hold. It felt like a book that was written straight through to be as creepy and engaging as possible, but whose plot and supporting characterizations were never checked for soundness. Disappointing.

What an odd book! I'm not sure if I liked it or not because I'm not sure exactly what happened. I get that it was about parents trying to protect their son from prosecution. I don't get why there was all these disjointed flashbacks about Paul, because although they gave insight into his character, they didn't really serve a purpose to the plot. I feel like there were too many unanswered questions and too many distractions to the plot for my liking.

book_b.title: Shadow and Bone (The Grisha, #1)
book_b.user_review:
This came highly recommended, which may be contributing to my slight sense of disappointment. "Shadow and Bone" is an acceptably good fantasy/magical yarn that resembles a number of books that came before it. Alina spends the book discovering that her magical power is even more powerful than first suspected, while sorting out the affections of two suitors. There are some minor charactors. Evil is battled. Magic happens. 
 Some reviewers have praised the proto-Russian flavor. Beyond that, I didn't find much here to really sell this book. The world-building is fine, just not memorable. The plot twists are fewer than I'd like. My big problem is that there's never serious doubt about the ending, and I think teen readers deserve to see something remarkable.

sample_reviews.review_text:
I don't know what I was expecting from this book, so many people talked about it so well, people whose tastes I share, I honestly believed I would like Shadow and Bone but what I got was a main character that was kind of boring, not very smart (though I wouldn't call her TSTL) and the "sorprising twist" I heard so much about was not much of a surprise to me. I saw it coming since their first conversations. 
 Just... I don't know what hype is all about.
Very enjoyable with great world building
What a delightful romp

** spoiler alert ** 
 I was unsure as to whether I would finish this book. On the one hand, the Internet absolutely raves about this series and I've heard very few bad things, but on the other hand, the first half of this book was just such a typical "special-snowflake-boarding-school" type of story - complete with our female lead slobbering all over some unattainably hot magical man and discovering her "true" super magically hot self after accepting her powers. All of that being said, though, the last third-or-so of this book really redeemed it and I am looking forward to reading the second. 
 Unfortunately, I'll be starting off on a negative note because the first good chunk of this book was so boring and annoying to me. Alina Starkov is a petulant child; an orphan, yes, but a petulant child all the same. She complains about everyyythinnngggg and is always in a sourpuss mood - which can be super-interesting for a character, but even when she's found to be a special snowwwflaaaake and Alina's living conditions skyrocket she still can't admit that it's not so bad being Grisha. She also falls head-over-heels for the most powerful Grisha (the Darkling) and even though she loves to point out to the reader how plain she is and how she doesn't deserve anything because she's so hiiiiideeeeouussssss, she never wonders why he falls for her so completely and so quickly. This annoyed me. Greatly. Their makeout scene in the castle made me just about roll my eyes out of my head. 
 Alina also had a fixation on beauty that was about to grate on my last nerve. The author works as a makeup artist (as per the author's blurb on the back flap) and, being a connoisseur of beauty enhancements myself, I was interested as to how she would weave beauty in with her story - especially after Alina mentioned her supposed plainness the first few times. There was a scene with Genya the magical makeup-makeover-artist that impressed me; where she explained to Alina that her makeover powers were temporary and didn't need to be abused to make people lovely. But Alinaaaaa omggggggg. There is more to a person than how beautiful they/you areeeeeeeee. Well, let me amend that statement: there is more to women than how beautiful they/you areeeeeee. Because Alina only ever commented on beauty when it had to do with women or the Darkling. Also Alina's only reason as to why she couldn't be a special-snowflake Grisha wasn't that she didn't have magical powers it was because omgggggg she's not prettyyyyyyyyyyyy. 
 Also also the prettiest Grisha, Zoya, was the bitchiest Grisha. Of course she was. 
 Let's move on to when I started to enjoy this story: PLOT TWIST TIME. 
 It wasn't one of those plot twists that made me go "OMG HOW DID I NEVER SEE THAT COMING MIND BLOWN OMGGGG", but it was more of "Omg I'm really glad the author also thought of this twist now everything is less annoying thank you". The Darkling is a manipulative, ruthless, greedy, power-hungry dick. Yes. Thank you, Leigh Bardugo. Thank you. This makes everything so much more interesting and makes the annoying parts relevant - the Darkling fooled Alina in to thinking that he cared for her, and as we are seeing this unfold through her POV we also believed him. 
 I also really liked Alina's childhood friend Mal and his confession of love to her. 
 One more flaw before I go, because it needs to be mentioned: even with my extremely limited knowledge of Russian culture and language, I could notice some blatant flaws in the author's interpretation of things like character names and especially kvas. And with a simple Google search I easily was able to double-check the rest of the cultural terms. So that was pretty irksome for me - I can only imagine how a Russian reader would feel! 
 I will continue with this series.
Could no put this down... it is such a good tale and had me crying at parts. I cannot wait till I read the next one!

Ever since Shadow and Bone was released, I've seen tons of reviews (and good ones at that) and everyone from bloggers to Barnes and Noble employes saying how great this book is and how they loved it and everyone should read it. But for some reason, I never really felt I wanted to read Shadow and Bone. I never felt that pull towards it and while I hate feeling felt out when it comes to books, I still didn't feel like I had to read this book. I just happened to see Shadow and Bone on BookOutlet.com and I couldn't say no. I put off reading Shadow and Bone for a couple months and I've told myself that this year I'll read all the books I've put off reading. Shadow and Bone was a the top of the list. 
 Shadow and Bone has a really cool core concept. I like the ideas and stuff but at the same time, there was a lot of things that weren't all that original. 
 The pace of the story was pretty great. I was never bored with the story. 
 The thing that's the biggest downer for me is I wasn't emotionally invested in the characters or the story. It wasn't until page 222 that I even had inner commentary. 
 Shadow and Bone is a great book but I just wasn't emotionally invested.
So much potential wasted.

A series that was supposed to be the next hunger games. I was lured in by the promise of a strong heroine, but what I got was a girl who gets by because of circumstance and the relationships she has with powerful men. She is supposed to have this power but it's so vague and stereotypical that I wasn't interested.

Actual rating: 3.5 
 I thought Shadow and Bone was really interesting. Where it fails to truly deliver is with the heroine, Alina. She comes off as nothing special, powers set aside. 
 There's a lot of ways to go from the ending and I'm definitely going to pick up the sequel.

reference_books.review_text:
I finally decided I'd read this. It was terribly boring. I suppose there was symbolism aplenty in it, but honestly, why bother? Symbolism is only important when it can bt put into a story you would like to read anyway. 
 Do teachers still force this down throats in high school? If they do, it's no wonder so few people like to read. The only point I can see to making any teenager read this book is to teach endurance!

reference_books.title: Eragon (The Inheritance Cycle, #1)
reference_books.review_text: The story here was interesting. The idea was a somewhat new and novel conglomeration of many sci-fi/fantasy themes in the past. The writing, however, felt very coarse. When I looked it up and found out that this book was written when the author was only 15, it made sense. The story was fun and entertaining, but the book itself could have used more polish. I'm planning to continue with the series, we'll see how it goes.

book_a.title: Making Money (Discworld, #36; Moist Von Lipwig, #2)
book_a.user_review:
This was a great book! It wasn't quite as good as "Going Postal" but I still want more of Moist! 
 I suspect part of the reason I loved this book so much is because a large portion of my childhood was spent listening to my father explain about the theory of money. The "Gold Standard" is something I was familiar with long before I hit middle school. Watching Pratchett has this all out was brilliant!

sample_reviews.review_text: "And with nods all around, this was the feeling of Tenth Egg Street. So long as the gold was somewhere, it kept banks honest and everything was okay. Moist felt humbled by such faith. If the gold was somewhere, herons would no longer eat frogs, either. But, in fact, there was no power in the world that could keep a bank honest if it didn't want to be" (p. 139).

Significantly better than Thud! and in some ways a lot like the earlier Discworld novels. 
 Aren't we due for another Death book?

Okay, guys, I really love Moist von Lipvig. Like, really love Moist von Lipvig. He's fantastic. Making Money made me so happy. I love him, and I love Adora Belle, because she's just so great!!! I love how much she is just completely her own person. 
 Okay really all y'all should just go read it. It deals with a pretty interesting follow-up to Moist's story in Going Postal. What happens to Moist when he's faced down all of his challenges at the post office? 
 Gosh, guys, I just love the characterization, and the world-building, and Pratchett's humor.

Pratchett starts with something we all take for granted (that those little green pieces of paper actually have value) and something most of think is really boring (basic economics), then bashes them over the head and runs away with them until you realize the one is much sillier and the other much more interesting than you ever could have thought. And he makes you laugh along the way. A lot.

Banking has never been so funny. 
 Moist von Lipwig becomes the boss of Ankh Morpork. Helped by the Chairman, who is also a dog, and Golems he transforms the bank, making more than a few enemies along the way. 
 Wonderful satire from Pratchett. Great characters, both new and old. 
 4 stars
i'm really still not sure whether or not i like moist von lipwig. which i guess is the point. i *do* like mr. fusspot. just for being named mr. fusspot. well, and for his favorite chew toy.

Hillarious as ever. I'm not sure there is much I can say about this book that I haven't already said before about Pratchett. Its funny, its smart, and its sharp as a tack. If you liked "Going Postal" I think you will enjoy this one, though its not quite as much of a rollercoaster ride. Still, we must remember that banks are much more dull than post offices.

I know so many people that adore this book and yes it is funny but for those who do not really get a tingle from cute humour; this may not intrigue you. Given the hints from the book 'Going Postal' I expected this book to have a deep uncovering of the nature of money, but there was a repetition of the money is an imaginative commodity which is not new but not entirely correct either. If you thought 'Pyramids' was not great, you will love this, and if 'Pyramids' was not great then I think you'll love this book.

Making Money is one of several Discworld books that grew on me - I didn't think too much of it after my first read, but subsequent re-reads have led to me enjoying it more and more as time passes. I think that quite a lot of that is due to the fact that Moist Von Lipwig is the protagonist, a character that can take a little getting used to. Nevertheless, he's loveable enough in his way, and certainly doing pretty well here. 
 In this novel, Moist receives a promotion of sorts, and he finds himself as the new boss of Ankh-Morpork's royal mint. As you can imagine, such a job doesn't come without its difficulties, and he finds himself placed in harm's way yet again by the benevolence of the patrician, Lord Vetinari. 
 Of course, this being an Ankh Morpork novel, there are plenty of familiar characters for the serious Discworld connoiseur to try to spot, and there are vampires to deal with, assassins to avoid and dogs to take for walkies. The city seems to have a mind of its own, and when it's introduced to paper currency for the first time, you know that something interesting is going to happen. 
 Lipwig is already known to Discworld fans as the Postmaster General of Ankh-Morpork - he managed to almost single-handedly resurrect the postal service, and so running a mint and a bank can't be too much of a problem, right? And he's doing it all reluctantly, as he did with the post office - in fact, there's an interesting story behind how that comes about. The previous owner leaves her shares to her dog in her will, and so her dog becomes the primary shareholder. She also leaves instructions that Moist is to be the dog's primary caregiver, and that he's to be killed by the assassin's guild if the dog dies or if he fails to take up the position. 
 It's an interesting predicament to be in, and the fact that he's forced to act against his will adds an extra dimension to the story. Moist Von Lipwig is one of those characters that we all love to hate - yes, he's a bit of a scoundrel, but so what? So is almost everyone on the Discworld, and it doesn't stop you from knowing them and loving them. And, as always, he's basically forced to run things through the sheer weight of his personality, which feels more developed than it does in almost any of his other characters. 
 Overall, Making Money is a joy to read, and it comes strongly recommended by me. It might not be the best introduction to the Discworld, but if you've read a few of the books before then it can't hurt to move on to this one.

I am hard pressed to choose my favorite Pratchett character. Tiffany Aching is certainly near the top of the list. And Death. And Susan, Death's granddaughter. And Rincewind. But after reading this book, I think Moist Von Lipwig moved up the list. Moist is wonderfully silly and wonderfully profound, and this book, if it fails to reach the level of satire that "Going Postal" achieved, it nonetheless manages to poke fun at macroeconomics and develop delicious characters in a page-turning and satisfying way. 
 I'm grateful for this latest Pratchett work especially with the recent news of his developing Alzheimer's Disease. Let's hope he continues in good health as long as possible and can give us many more of these hilarious books.

book_b.title: The Bad Beginning (A Series of Unfortunate Events, #1)
book_b.user_review:
As popular as this series is.... I just really didn't get into it. The whole thing was just... well, depressing! I guess the title could have fortold that, but I'm not one who really enjoys books without happy endings. 
 It was well written, however, and probably does appeal to people who are less emotionally attached to what they read. lol.. I can't even watch embarassing situations in TV without getting a stomach ache and wanting to leave the room!

sample_reviews.review_text: I hate this book. Presumably, it is supposed to be funny? But I don't understand how three children being horribly mistreated is funny. I found it completely unsettling.

What did I learn from this book? That when he says this book is unhappy, he really, REALLY means it. It's a miserable piece of writing, and it utterly fails to involve me. I'm only glad it was a gift, so I didn't have to pay for it.

I have been wanting to read this for awhile, and finally picked up a set of the first 3 books on Kindle for $2.99. I couldn't pass that up, and since I had enjoyed the movie I figured it was pretty much a given that I would enjoy the books as well. I was not wrong. I highly enjoyed reading this. It's a fun and light read. :) 
 Likely to read rest of series: Definitely.

3.5 stars. 
 I like the way this was written, and the three clever characters Violet, Klaus, and Sunny. I really only give it 3.5 stars because I am not a fan of books that do not have happy endings. It was an entertaining and quick read. The evil foster parent situation reminded me of James & the Giant Peach, which I read many times as a child and was semi-obsessed with.. So I do think I may continue to read this series and see what will happen next to the Baudelaire children.
What are you to do when the author says unfortunate things will happen and that there is no happy ending? Well you go on and read of course....

Whoaaa. I wish I read this as a kid! I loved this! Gothic and postmodern. I like how the narrator is also a character in the book. I also like how as much as the author talks down to the audience...it deals with dark themes like death and pain. I think that it's a great book for kids, it will enhance their vocabulary but its not so dark that they will be traumatized. It's even really funny!
I remember reading this series back when i was a little girl. It was like the first 'big' series that i read.

I wish I had of read this book when I was younger because I think it would have fascinated me alot more. However, I liked how Snicket explained the words he was using. I think this book and the rest of the Series of Unfortunate Events would be good books for children to read because of the way he describes bigger words to make it easier for children to understand. All in all it is a good childrens' book.
I am reading this on my Nook. It is ..... interesting. I saw the movie and read enough reviews either loving or hating the book that I was intrigued.

I've been hearing about this series since like forever. Thank God for Scribd, all 10 or 13 books in the series are there, and I intend to finish them... 
 I told my younger cousin, Ore, that I was reading this first book. He started laughing hard and said Snicket was a sadist...he had read it when he was 13 or 14.. 
 All in all, I enjoyed the book and his weird style. I don't know who he is yet, but I suspect he had a hard childhood, and this is his way of telling other children that life is not always rosy. 
 Fun stuff. 5 solid stars.

book_a.user_review:
4.5/10 
 Just an average book hyped unnecessarily.

sample_reviews.review_text: First book of 2012! Literally couldn't put it down and read all in one go. Great concept; and I love a strong female protagonist who is unapologetically manipulative without being vilified, mediagenic without being overly sexualized. Deftly critiques politics of oppression and a heartless, self-absorbed entertainment industry. Action-packed, with tons of dynamic visuals - will make a great movie (scheduled for release in march). Thanks to my niece and nephew for loaning me your copy!
Suspenseful story, very very interesting. The ending though kinda was bleh!! It will get me to read the sequel, though, for sure!

This really is a good read. Recently there have been many truly excellent young adult titles, but popularity is no guarantee of excellence, so I wasn't expecting much, and I have been more than pleasantly surprised. After feeling resistant to the first page or two, the book won me over. Who doesn't love a good survival story? I began to find the narrator's voice is very appealing, the way she can figure things out. Always great to have a strong, capable female protagonist. I like that she comes from Appalachia and has all those nature skills. Also, I guess it doesn't hurt that I like reality TV - I think the author is spot on in creating a future that present-day readers can really relate to, by giving us a survival reality TV show set in a post-apocalyptic world.
I've never watched an entire episode of Survivor, but this book is an interesting juxtaposition of Lord of the Flies and reality TV. Much edgier that her Gregor series. I can't wait for the sequel.

The Hunger Games is a controversial young adult dystopian novel that is a highly competitive death-dealing game, and a fight for survival. I couldn't watch the film - there wasn't enough to grab my attention - but the book was bought as a gift and was the only dystopian one on my shelf. As a result, I didn't begin reading with much expectation that I would take to the novel: I'm not a fan of the young adult genre in general, with some exceptions. 
 The novel had quite a potent political message, especially early on. It illustrates simply and yet strongly how inequality can lead to resentment between the starving and the better-off, even if both groups know better on a full stomach. It's a clever ploy of the Capitol's system to divide the people so that their hold on power is relatively undisrupted. The Capitol uses official excuses for those who have starved to death, burying their guilt and complicity at ridding many of the districts of their inhabitants. The population are not fooled, but what can they do to act against the Capitol when the Treaty of Treason is an intimidating warning to those who would oppose them, in the form of a reminder that past uprisings have bitterly failed. It's at this point the reader must wonder how accurate this history is, and if it is, why do the Capitol need to remind the districts not to rebel if there weren't weaknesses? 
 Let's start with the positive. There were more than a few lengthy passages that sustained my interest, mostly between Katniss and Peeta's struggle to understand and trust each other before they entered the Hunger Games as the two Tributes representing District 12. The battle for survival in the arena started off very well, capturing my interest and impressing upon me the severity of Katniss' predicament. The conclusion as well, was well written, emotionally tense, and with enough peril to make it impressive. First-person point-of-view worked well at intervals, bringing Katniss' personality, likes, and dislikes to the fore and engaging the reader. 
 Katniss' voice did bother me, rendering her emotionally numb to any related or past events. This is where first-person point-of-view didn't work well, and the switches were occasionally noticeable. Katniss and Peeta's mostly passive and tolerant attitude to following rules irritated me. I know why they did it - to protect their families - but it almost seemed to justify the need for a sycophantic totalitarian regime, bloated by wealth and superficiality. It made the characters sick, and it made me feel sick, but the characters still went along with it more often that I would have liked. I'm obviously only commenting as a reader/observer here and not a participant in the Hunger Games; maybe that would make a difference to my opinions. 
 Katniss's boundaries were pushed once or twice, causing her to act in rebellion, but her actions only really made a difference where it concerned the Capitol's perception of her and to me reinforced the idea that if you have enough talent you can become popular enough that it doesn't matter that most districts are starved and oppressed. The bottom line is that Katniss and Peeta were absolutely helpless, and had to do as they were told. I didn't think this philosophy did much to encourage young adults in life, even if the suspense and gory deaths were appealing to some.

When I saw the movie with my daughter I knew I needed to read the books. I think it would be difficult to review this book without having read the series, and I recommend reading all three books. I will not detail the plot or charaters, as these are welll known at this point. As a series they are well written and the first person narrative is perfect for the nature of the story. As Borges once noted, the amount of suffering that can be known and understood at one time by a person is that of one other person. We cannot feel the suffering of millions save through the suffering of one. The Hunger Games trilogy makes this clear. 
 The Hunger Games is part a young adult read, part adult cautionary tale. Read alone, which it can be, it is a reflection on how children can be used to punish the sins of their parents while keeping the parents under political and economic control. It can be read as ancritique of current times. My 12yo daughter saw this clearly, which was startling. 
 A final note-- There has been some critique that the second book, Catching Fire, was not as good as the other two, but that is not the case.

Firstly I want to say I didn't particularly want to read The Hunger Games. I have found that books with such hype around them are rarely that good. However my husband who is incredibly critical read the book and liked it and recommended I did the same. So I gave it a go. 
 I have to say that I was presently surprised; despite the slow start (I found Part 1 slightly unbearable) the story really got going once the contestants hit the arena and the Hunger Games began. Set in a dystopian North America the Hunger Games are used to control the population of twelve districts which surround the Capitol. Two children/teenagers are picked every year from each district to fight to the death while the population watches. 
 This was all round a good story, Katniss (the heroine) is actually quite badass (Bella from Twilight could learn a lot) which is refreshing. The action sequences are exciting and the conclusion of the book seems to lead nicely to the second book, although obviously I know this is a trilogy so that point is irrelevant. All in all I enjoyed.
Finished this book in one day bc I could not put it down. Keeps your attention from the very first page.
AMAZING BOOK OMY GOSH I LOVE IT
Hated it. Don't know what all the fuss is about. Tried to read it, got really really bored, disliked the main character intensely.

book_b.title: Leviathan Wakes (The Expanse, #1)
book_b.user_review:
First, it was the 4 point something rating.....and then the praise by George Martin. 
 I had to pick it up; just to leave it halfway. Bad characters and a cheesy plot. Detective Miller gets obsessed with Julie Mao without any reason. I mean he didn't even start investigating her for a month maybe. How can you get obsessed so easily? Disappointment. 
 No space opera for sometime now.

sample_reviews.review_text: I'd call this a 'hard' Sf space opera, the science and space flight mechanics feel realistic and they wrap round a compelling story. Jim Holden is a bit of an idiot but I wanted if to come through and I felt very engaged with the characters. Plus lots of stuff go boom!
Epic. Some critical elements not consistent or scientifically accurate.

Yeah, so I was so nose-deep in this one that I almost sailed past my train stop. Dammit. 
 What makes it good? For me, it's the strong dialogue, coupled with likable characters. The premise of the book is a pleasant mix of different ideas brought together in a cogent whole. It's not *just* about a virus. It's not *just* about star ships. It's not *just* about politics and racism. It's all of those, bound up together against a huddle of people who are just trying to get by. 
 Like many believable heroes, they struggle against being in the wrong (or right) place at the wrong time. They each respond to the call differently. The Butcher of Anderson Station is quite a different man from Detective Miller, but they're both really just trying to save life as we know it. I can get behind that. 
 I mentioned dialogue before, and it's a strong point worth raising again. It's not just that the people in here are individuals with their own motivations, but that the langauge and way they speak is different. The Belter dialect is superb, mixing language in a way you can almost feel. I've no clue what it's supposed to mean but it fits well with the story and the people who use it. I hesitate to mention it, but I'm an author too: it's this kind of realism that I tried for in my book Night's Favour, because it rides right to the core of the reader and makes it real. 
 What I really like is the happy ending isn't saccarine and trite. Not everyone can make it out alive in a situation like this, and it's not happily ever after. But it *is* happy, and the right things happen to the right people, in kinda the right ways. The story had so many moving parts I wasn't sure if it could be closed so readily, but the authors nailed it. Nice work. 
 ...I've just fired the rest of "Corey's" works to my Kindle. I can't wait to see what the authors do next.

Pretty great space opera. It skirts around the edges of annoying hard science fiction--characters are obsessed with gravity; they never stop thinking or talking about--but the story trucks along fast enough that I was able to get over what would have been a showstopper otherwise.

Kick ass space opera in the tradition of Peter Hamilton without the characters getting out of hand. Hell of a fun start to the series! Loved Miller's wit and even though Holden is a bit holier than thou, loved the entire crew of the Rocinante.

To date, this series has been one book after another of fantastic, well-thought out, engagingly written, perfectly believable, near future, in-system (although this changes somewhat as time goes on, so far there is always still a lot happening "here at home") space opera. If that sounds like your thing, then I can't imagine you not liking these books. One of the best collaborative efforts I've read in a long time.

The two main characters, Miller and Holden, are about as trite as they come, and Holden is unlikeable to boot. Like a preachy Han Solo with all the rogueish charm removed and replaced with Righteous Indignation (the most boring kind). 
 My way of looking at things is, you have to have likeable characters, or you have to have amazing writing. The writing in this book is only OK. Sorry, I didn't enjoy reading this book, and I won't continue the series.

Sci-fi is a lot like pizza, wherever you find it its always made up of the same basic ingredients but the quality can vary immensely depending on who's doing the cooking and I can happily tell you that Leviathan Wakes is some damn good pizza. 
 ...Sorry the whole pizza analogy sounded way better in my head. Anyway, yeh its a great book even if it does seem to have been going down the Sci-fi tropes check list (Ragtag crew caught up in events bigger than they could imagine? Check. Tense interplanetary political situation that threats to plunge humanity into civil war? Double check. Amoral corporations using alien technology to dubious ends? Triple check). 
 The story is told from the perspectives of Holden and Millar, two men looking at the universe from opposite ends. Both are likable characters but I did find Millar much more interesting - a ageing cop striving to find a purpose but hampered by a overly cynical world view and a moral compass warped by a life of too many hard knocks. 
 The book is set within the confines of our solar system - mankind has reached the outer planets but not the stars. This means the setting is grand enough to create a sense of awe but close enough to home that the stakes feel real once the shit hits the hyperdrive. It has a nice lived in quality and plenty of thought has gone into the day to day details of life out in the solar system. Leviathan Wakes is very much the best action/adventure I've read in ages and I'd recommend it to pretty much everybody.

An absolutely enthralling new world by the author duo. It has action, suspense, drama and good old sci-fi elements neatly blended in. It's a must read for everyone looking to delve into modern sci-fi. Looking forward to the whole Expanse series ! 
 My rating: 4.5/5

Good sci-fi. Reads a lot like a mystery novel. Dialogue isn't the best, but I was swept along with the story enough that I'm committed to reading the next book in this series. Many gave this book 4 stars. I just read NIGHT FILM, a masterpiece, so perhaps I'm jaded...Still, I'm giving this 3 stars.

reference_books.title: Wifey
reference_books.review_text:
Judy Blume's first book geared towards adults. I hated it! I wish I could give it negative stars here. It's such a shame since I remember really liking her books as a child and recommending her to my own girls. 
 I loathed every character in this book (who were poorly introduced by the way, and left me wondering if I missed something "Who ARE these people?"). The husband is a complete @$$. There are the types of meddlesome parents/in-laws that complain about the names given to their new grandchildren. 
 I'm no prude but I found the vulgar language used to describe the main character's own anatomy offensive... What is Blume trying to do here? Shock us? Slap us in the face as if to say "Hey look, this is NOT a kid's book"? 
 According to the introduction by Blume the main character dumps the husband and goes on an adventure... But by the fourth chapter I didn't care about her enough to hang around and see if she grew some ovaries and started acting like a real woman or not. In all fairness, there was sort-of a humorous part and I'm hoping it gets much much better after chapter four (I just wasn't going waste my time in any case). So if you read it... did it? Get any better?

Years later my sister-in-law gave me a whole stack of books from this series starting with "Witness". I started reading it out of boredom and decided I better go back to "Glory". Now I'm hooked! Maybe I'll go back and give this one another read.

I thought this was a good book, although not as fast-paced as some of the installments in the series. It was interesting and I enjoyed it, especially the brief visit to Ireland. Loved seeing Roarke and Eve working together yet again:)
Love this series, it's easy to read with great characters, enough said!
Always enjoy J D Robb but found this one a bit repetitive e.g. Eve's attitude to those with old money and them using the same techniques to trap the killers. Still enjoyed it though.

It is unbelievably fascinating to say that the Naked in Deaththe first book in the series and where all the romance started and probably got married in the 3rd book, Immortal in Death; the former was published 1995 and the latter 1996. I could not argue with how Miss J.D. Robb was able to pull off with all the development of the compelling characters as this 31st installment was made 15 years after. The first few chapters of this installment made me realize as Eve and Roarke just only celebrated their 2nd wedding anniversary. Imagine that?! And imagine all the crimes already in mind and how I mustered investigative techniques and observed people and mastered the being a kickass. J.D. Robb perfectly well was a police officer in her previous life. 
 As amazing as Roarke is, this book started with hot Irish vacation and all the Irish lilts. It was just enthralling how Eve caught a crime in Ireland and how she managed to help a neophyte police officer solving a case. Life goes on for Eve as she faced another crime of indulgences of the rich and selfish individuals. Yes, I should say that the resolution of the crime was quite dragging. Eve came round and round as she unraveled the motives of the crimes. Only that I love how Eve projected and baited herself to capture her suspects. Just like a friend, I was very proud of Eve luring her suspects under her power and giving a full kickass kickback to ego-feed her killers. 
 Another way to love this book too is the progress of Eve's relationship to her friends as this book ended with a Saturday Barbeque Party courtesy of Eve. Being so concerned and wanted to catch up with Morris who maybe was recuperating from the death of Detective Coltraine in the Promises in Death. Eve had shown her courage to show concern to a friend and even shocked for she even could not believe herself falling and was able to manage well in the friendship department.

Another okay book in the Eve Dallas series - I think Robb's writing is good, the plots are good - but Eve and Roarke are getting old. Every book we rehash all of their emotional issues and past, and I'm getting tired of going through it every time. I think I'll lay off of Robb for awhile and see if I can work up any enthusiasm for the series after that.
I'll probably have to re-read this as it is far ahead from the other books I read. I liked this book, but I'm not sure it has all the same drive as some of the other books. Its still good.

Oddly when Columbo starts a mystery and we know who the killer is I don't mind it. I do, for some reason, mind it, when I'm reading mysteries so when we know halfway through who the killers are I wasn't very happy. 
 And I had trouble with some of the things between Eve and Roarke this time. She seemed oddly overdependent on him.

I'm amazed that Nora Roberts (J.D. Robb) has managed to keep this series consistently entertaining for 30+ books. Indulgence in Death was another strong entry in this series, with some great humor, dialogue, suspense, and pacing. 
 Other reviewers have mentioned that the mystery was a bit similar to a previous book, but it didn't really bug me, the suspense was tight enough that I didn't notice the similarity until after I finished Indulgence in Death. I zipped through this book in one sitting, then went back to reread some of my favorite parts. 
 I enjoy the mysteries in the In Death series, but what keeps me reading this series are the relationships. Roarke and Eve are a fantastic romantic pairing. I love watching them falling in love, then adjusting to the give and take that takes place in a relationship, and learning to become a couple. I also love the friendships between characters as well, I like that Eve goes from being a bit of a recluse to having a wider circle of friends. Her bafflement at trying to understand the various relationships in her life is touching and very funny. 
 The humor was top notch in this book, and I thoroughly enjoyed Eve's discomfort with too much nature, potentially armed farm animals, and little kids. 
 I'm happy that Roberts writes so quickly, cause I can't wait for the next In Death book. 
 Grade: 4.5 stars

sample_reviews.review_text: The murder hits close to home this time and a cop killer is on the loose. I enjoyed this one.
One emotional read and another unforgettable character development for Eve as far as dealing with friendship is concerned.

I am reading this book for a book club - someone wanted us to talk about a mystery and this was the one chosen. I would suggest that you not read it unless you have read others in the series. I was 1/3 through the book when I found out that it was the 28-29th in a series and is set in the future. I was quite confused because I had not read any of the previous books in the series. 
 This may have been a big part of my feelings about the book but I was really out of my comfort zone in the genre. I like historical fiction - this was the other end of the spectrum. 
 I congratulated myself when I kept reading until the end - but it was from determination and not enjoyment. I guess it is well written - I am not a good judge. It is a female woman detective who is working on the case of the murder of another female policewoman. Quite a few twists and turns but she does solve it. I read other reviews that said they guessed the killer in advance - not me. Maybe that was because I am not a mystery aficionado. (Truth is I am not sure how to spell that word.)

I can't remember now who first got me reading J. D. Robb's series about Eve Dallas and Roarke (although I suspect the blame can be laid at the feet of "Barbara the bookseller" who has sold me a lot of books in the series since then). It doesn't really matter. I'm hooked. I love Eve and Roarke and their ever developing relationship and I enjoy the futuristic setting and the murder mysteries to be solved. So when I heard there was a new one coming out I slapped a reserve on it at the library (I buy this series, but in paperback - I'd be broke by now if I bought it in hardcover!). 
 Eve finds herself with a personal stake in her latest case when the victim turns out to be the girlfriend of Li Morris, the NYSPD ME and a good friend. She is reluctantly forced to look into the possibility Amaryllis Coltraine may have been a dirty cop, even as she works to bring the killer to justice and deal with the intrusion of an old enemy into her and Roarke's lives. 
 Robb's books are always fun reads, but their quality does vary from enjoyable right through to excellent. Happily, Promises in Death is up at the excellent end of the scale. 
 There is a good, solid mystery. It's not so simple the reader can easily solve it, but not so twisty you need notes to figure everything out. The clues and progress of the case are clearly laid out and Eve works steadily towards the solution while still finding time for her own life and time with Roarke. Of course, these books are always more about the progress of the case and the relationships rather than solving the mystery. I don't remember if I ever tried to figure out "whodunnit" when I read them, but I certainly don't now. Instead, I just go along for the ride and enjoy whatever Robb decides to throw at me. In this case there's a lovely balance of work and play and a light tossing of angst as Eve tries to deal with Morris's grief and his need to be part of the case even through she knows he's not the tiniest bit objective. 
 It's all balanced very well. It was also nice to see Eve and Roarke simply working together without their issues providing the angst this time. While that can provide a great story, it's also a pleasure just to see them interacting. There is a wonderful scene where, as they begin to realise an old enemy is involved, both promise not to antagonise the other - then they acknowledge that they probably won't actually manage to do it and proceed to make up (or should that be make out?) in advance. 
 But most priceless scene is Eve's reaction when she is left to host Louise's hen party while Roarke takes Charles and a large number of friends to Las Vegas (Eve is horrified enough that they're taking the innocent Trueheart, then she nearly has a heart attack as she realised Roarke will be taking Mr Mira to a strip club). Her plea to go with them and Roarke's response is just wonderful and a total laugh out loud moment. 
 In the end, I did actually find myself feeling rather sorry for the murderer, something that isn't usually the case, but this individual was actually rather pathetic in a vicious way and Eve's method of resolving the case was harsh but brilliant. 
 All in all, Promises in Death is an excellent addition to the series and one I thoroughly enjoyed reading. 
 Promises in Death 
 J. D. Robb 
 Eve and Roarke, Book 34 
 9/10

I enjoyed it. Eve and Rourke's relationship mellowed out in this one, I think the point was to see them settle into a REAL marriage and, although I loved the tormented and torrid earlier books, there was something nice about seeing them settle in and be happy without drama, be partners and comfortable together. I can see the baby on the horizon, 2-3 books down the line, and it's really time. The mystery was quite good too, very heartfelt because it was close to a character we know. Really enjoyed it!

Not my favorite when it comes to the killings/mystery because it wasn't nearly bloody, violent, and sinister enough. But, the good part of this book was that there was plenty of attention paid to all of the side-characters of the series that we have grown to know and love. 
 So, cop-killer pursuit - meh. a little boring. Plus, I figured out who the first bad-guy was as soon as we met, and the second bad-guy as soon as we knew there was another. Come on, man! Give me a challenge!! 
 Dead cop's boyfriend story - touching and sad. He is a character that I have always liked. I know, let's kill the love of his life! Sinister authors with their emotional manipulation. Humph! 
 Eve & Roarke - amazing and cute. Eve was actually not a bitch in this book and even treated her husband well enough for me to almost approve. (I would treat him better. Just sayin') 
 Eve hosting a bridal shower/bachelorette party - only funny because she was so awkward and hated it. Of course, Peabody was the best part. I like drunk Peabody! Actually I like everyone when I'm drunk. 
 Roarke taking a giant group of guys to Vegas - money. Why, oh why, did we have to stay at the chick party instead of getting to go to Vegas with them? 
 "I'm taking a shuttle full of men to Las Vegas late this afternoon. There will be ribaldry, and a possible need to post bond. I've made arrangements. I'll bring back this same shuttle full of men - hopefully - tomorrow afternoon." 
 "Let me come with you." 
 "Let me see your penis." 
 "Oh, God! Can't I just use yours?" 
 "At any other time." 
 Oh, and just in case you are as ignorant as I am: 
 rib*ald 
 'rib@ld,'ri,bold 
 adjective 
 referring to sexual matters in an amusingly rude or irreverent way. 
 "a ribald comment" 
 That makes it funnier, huh? Huh? 
 Yeah, I totally want to go to Vegas and have ribaldy fun with my girl-tribe.

I took a bit of a break from the series for a few months, because they were starting to feel repetitive to me. Jeff Lindsay's Dexter, Dean Koontz's Odd Thomas, just to name a few. I'm glad I took the break! Roarke and Eve seem "fresh" yet "familiar" to me. And I was anxious to see what kind of trouble they could get into now.... 
 First, the sex scenes are getting more glossed over, which is really a bit more true-to-life, anyway, don't you think? Eve & Roarke have been married for almost 2 years now. In the last several books the sex scenes were frequent, and really rather harsh and raw. C'mon... NO woman wants it like that ALL the time, and not many men out there would even want to keep up that pace for that long. So this is more like it :) Yeah, they are still in love, yeah, the sex is still super hot, and yeah, they like to bang each other on a fairly regular basis. But we, the audience, are really just catching their afterglows now. 
 Something I DON'T like, that I thought was just a one-time thing that happened a few books back, and has now become something of a norm at least once in every book since, is how Eve has stopped having nightmares (that part is a good thing....) but that her dreams are now becoming somewhat prophetic. 
 Really? Eve? A psychic? NOT! I can appreciate the subconscious working the facts out during sleeptime (good grief, does she EVER stop working?), but there have been more than one occasion where something very small will happen or be said in her dreams that is not based on her investigation to date, and is more prophetic. Seems a bit on the campy side for our practical-no-nonsense Lieutenant....

This book broke my heart just a little for Morris. What a great story. This book had me cracking up one minute & riping my heart to pieces the next. 
 Just when I think the series can't get any better - it does.

I loved everything about this addition to the in Death series, including the coral cover which just screams...It's summer...read me! Whereas I was quite disappointed in the previous release, Salvation in Death, this one satisfied on all fronts. Eve seems much more comfortable being a wife, yet much still baffles her about life and relationships. The connection between Eve and Roarke was much more focused on with Eve experiencing a series of revelations or conclusions about herself and their relationship. I felt Eve really grew in this novel as a person and as a cop. 
 In Salvation in Death I thought the book lacked on the emotional front. Well, Promises in Death more than makes up for it. Eve responds to a call and finds the body of murdered Detective Amarylis Coltraine, the woman that her friend Medical Examiner Morris had been dating for the past year. I reread the first 20 pages of the book a few times and it made me want to break out crying every time. Although the story focuses on a devastating event there were a lot of funny moments too. Especially Eve describing the goings on at Louise's bachelorette party. There seemed to be more snarling, witty, and snappy dialogue than usual too, a feature I have come to anticipate from every Robb novel. 
 Promises in Death deals with a deeper and more complex crime involving a criminal from Eve and Roarke's past. Robb ponders the sins of the father and what a son or daughter make of their life with the family they have been dealt. I think "Promises" in Promises in Death means Eve's promise to Morris to find Coltraine's killer...Eve's and Roarke's promise to each to always communicate and for each to make the right decisions even when those decisions are difficult. I thought this was one of the best in Death books. Would have liked a final subconscious conversation from Eve between her and Coltraine after she brings down the murderer. I'm interested to see where Robb takes the series from here and plan to read the newest release Kindred in Death.

Chief Medical Examiner Morris loses his lover to murder. Clearly the roots of Amaryllis's murder lie in her past, but Eve has run up against her main suspect before, and he is following his same pattern. She just has to find out who is acting on his behalf. It's going to be a very satisfying take-down.

reference_books.title: The Heir (The Selection, #4)
reference_books.review_text:
I knew that for my sake--for my family's sake--I had to finish my Selection. And, when I did, I'd have a ring on my finger. 
 I wasn't expecting that I'd actually enjoy this book. I got this book and left it unread for quite some time, merely because in my opinion The Selection is a trilogy, not a multi novella that has no end. The plot is light and easy, anyone could've guessed it easily. A kinda spoiled and bitchy heir, Princess Eadlyn who had no intention of getting married or falling in love was forced into a selection to find a husband. She insisted that she didn't want it at first stubbornly and as the story goes on she finally had a change of heart at the end. Cliche and boring. 
 What makes me enjoy this book is honestly the characters. They are not deep and so well-developed. But I like the way the Selected are portrayed as an ordinary man with something special within them. I believe that everyone does have it, either they're a commoner or a member of Royal Family. Thought America and Maxon' character falls boring and flat after 20 years. I'm not going to say anything about the main character, Eadlyn since she really has nothing special that caught my attention. I honestly think at the end of this series, I'd have nothing worth remembering except for the fluffy and easy feelings I got while reading. 
 It's still recommended if you're looking for a real quick and light read to get forgotten easily later on.

reference_books.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 Saya tidak tahu harus bagaimana mendeskripsikan Montase. Saya sudah membaca hampir semua karya Windry Ramadhina dan yang satu ini benar-benar exceptional. Montase berputar sekitar dunia perfilman, spesifiknya film dokumenter. Namun, bukan topik ini yang membuat saya begitu menyukai buku ini, tapi cara penulis menceritakan kecintaan seorang Rayyi terhadap film dokumenter, rintangan yang dihadapinya, sampai akhirnya mimpi laki-laki itu tercapai. Tidak lupa akan Haru, seorang gadis Jepang yang membawa dampak besar dalam kehidupan Rayyi. Jujur, di awal cerita saya kurang menyukai tokoh Haru yang ceroboh dan kekanakan, sama sekali bukan sikap yang ditunjukkan seorang gadis berusia kepala dua. Misalnya di halaman 160: "Dia (Haru) meninggalkan gerbang stasiun dengan berlari kecil dan melompat beberapa kali", melompat? Seriously? Hanya karena langit mendung? Tapi seiring berjalannya cerita, mau tidak mau saya kagum pada "gadis dengan senyum perahu naga" dan semangatnya dalam menjalani sisa hidupnya. Haru yang melepas mimpinya untuk melukis hanya dengan kalimat singkat "Selalu ada impian yang lebih besar dari impian lain". Saya suka cara Windry menuliskan tentang kepergian Haru, dengan singkat dan jelas. Tidak dengan adegan di kamar rumah sakit yang penuh dengan dialog cheesy sambil berpegangan tangan. 
 Secara keseluruhan, Montase bernuansa sendu, namun tidak mendayu-dayu. Selipan dialog antara Rayyi dengan teman-temannya (Google V) selalu meringankan suasana. Alurnya agak lambat, namun tidak membosankan. Sederhana dan gaya penulisannya cukup berbeda dari karya Windry lainnya. Saya serasa membaca tulisan Winna Efendi (penulis Refrain), mungkin karena suasana dan atribut Jepang yang dibawakan Haru? Hahaha 
 Jika ada hal yang disayangkan dari Montase, buat saya pribadi adalah hubungan ayah-anak Rayyi dengan ayahnya. Saya rasa bagian itu masih bisa digali lebih jauh, misalnya mengapa ayah Rayyi tidak menyukai film dokumenter padahal itu adalah kesukaan istrinya? Apakah ada alasan lain dibandingkan sekedar "film dokumenter tidak memiliki masa depan" ataukah ada hal lain? Saya juga ingin mengetahui penyelesaian dari konflik ayah-anak tersebut. Misalnya pembicaraan empat mata yang membuat ayah Rayyi akhirnya mendukung Rayyi akan mimpinya. 
 Sejauh ini, saya hanya menemukan sebuah typo. Halaman 248: "Dua kepal nasi Jepang" membuat saya mengerutkan dahi sejenak, oh ternyata kata "kepal" tertukar urutannya dengan "nasi".

reference_books.title: Eleanor & Park
reference_books.review_text:
"That's what people say--'it's not good-bye'--when they're too afraid to face what they're really feeling. I'm not going to see you tomorrow, Park--I don't know when I'll see you again. That deserves more than 'it's not goodbye'" 
 This is not an average love story you'll find in YA romance. This isn't about a popular jock and an outcast girl' love story. The guy doesn't tell the girl that she's the most beautiful girl in the world. They don't have sex every single weekend. It's not a love-hate relationship. It's more than that.. 
 The story sets in August 1986, Park is half-Korean and Eleanor is a white and redheaded Danish and they met on the bus. Eleanor was weird in Park's eyes, and always is (in a good way). And Park makes Eleanor feel like she wants to eat his face. Their love started from comics and music tapes and separated in Minnesota: 
 I don't love this book, it definitely isn't my favorite romance YA. Some pages are boring and until the end there isn't anything that makes my heart beats faster or else. It's an ordinary love you had when you're 17, their love isn't about forever and ever. It could just be a fling and a year later everything could change. She doesn't call him her boyfriend, she only says 'I love you' once on page 325/325. But what pulls me into this book is that it's realistic, like we're young and haven't been in our 20s yet so we could love and date someone we met on the school bus, and even at the end we won't be together, it's still a good love to remember in our old days. For me, this book is just 3-stars, a neutral rating. It's not special and extraordinary but it's just "Eleanor and Park"

sample_reviews.review_text:
Novel yang dikemas dengan format berbeda dan unik ini membuat penasaran setiap menyimak cerita dari enam orang; tentang kedekatan mereka dengan Itsumi dan penyebab kematian Ketua Klub Sastra itu. Setiap ceritanya sering menyuguhkan fakta berbeda yang membuat bingung sekaligus penasaran. Ini resensi lengkap saya: 
 http://dinoybooksreview.wordpress.com...

sebagai penakut yang gak akan mau baca/nonton film horor ( kecuali terpaksa/dipaksa), gue mau membuat pengakuan, bahwa, rasa penasaran bisa mengalahkan rasa takut. 
 setelah cukup penasaran dengan novel ini beberapa waktu lalu akhirnya dapet juga. 
 Novel ini keren! 
 kenapa? karena ditiap bab kita disuguhnkan dengan kemungkinan-kemungkinan siapa yg jadi dalang pembunuhan, memojokan semua pihak, bukan mengacu pada satu orang. sampai di bab terakhir pun kita dibuat tercengang. loh kok bisa? pasti banyak yg ngomong gitu pas selesai baca, yakan? 
 Keren, horor plus main detektif-detektifan :D

Yandere. 
 Cuma itu yang bisa saya bilang di sini. 
 Ceritanya sih bagus, kejutannya mantap, tapi kalau boleh jujur, ini bukan tipe yang bikin perasaan nyaman setelah baca...

Terkadang sesuatu yang terlihat begitu sempurna ternyata menyimpan rahasia besar di dalamnya. Tapi dalam novel ini yang tersimpan sebagai rahasia itu bukan sesuatu yang indah, tapi mengerikan. Rahasia besar dalam Klub Sastra SMA Putri Santa Maria. 
 Novel ini terdiri dari enam cerita pendek yang ditulis dan dibacakan oleh seluruh anggota klub. Uniknya, ritual pembacaan karya tulis ini saat pertemuam rutin yang bertema yami-nabe. Cara penulisan Akiyohi Rikako ini termasuk fresh dan segar menurutku. Cara pembukaan kisahnya pun unik. Aku sebagai pembaca merasa duduk bersama mereka para tokoh dan diajak mendengarkan mereka yang sedang menceritakan kisahnya. Coba rasakan sendiri deh sensasinya saat baca novel ini. >_< 
 Tapi novel ini buatku biasa aja misterinya. Aku pun bisa menebak semua teka teki di novel ini yang dibuktikan pada pembacaan cerita terakhir. When my deduction is true, I feel like I'm a Sherlock Holmes. Hahaha 
 Eh ada yang meleset sih perkiraannya satu doang. Beyond expectation. 
 Mungkin karena genre macam begini adalah bacaan favoritku, dan sudah membaca berbagai karya novel yang lebih bertema berat dari ini, jadi aku menganggap Girls in the Dark ini gak terlalu memukau. 
 Ada banyak clue di setiap babnya. Aku sebenernya bisa memaparkan clue yang berceceran itu. But, I wan't spoil you. Kasian yang belum baca. Hihi baca sendiri aja deh yaah. ;) 
 Aku recommend buku karya Akiyoshi Rikako ini buat kalian yang gak suka misteri tapi pengen coba baca genre misteri. Buku ini cocok buat bacaan awal kalian, itung-itung pemanasan. Karena konflik dan cara penulisannya ringan untuk ukuran genre misteri. 
 3.5 stars

Adalah Shiraishi Itsumi, seorang bintang di sebuah sekolah katolik khusus putri, meninggal setelah terjatuh dari lantai dua sekolah dengan posisi memegang bunga lili. Tidak ada penghuni sekolah yang tahu kenapa dan bagaimana seorang gadis cantik, pintar, paling popular seantero sekolah meninggal dengan keadaan seperti itu, tidak ada, kecuali mungkin keenam anggota klub sastra ekslusif yang dihidupkan kembali oleh sang ketua Shiraishi Itsumi. 
 Novel ini diawali dengan premis adanya misteri dibalik kematian Shiraishi Itsumi, yang kemudian untuk memperingati kematiannya, Klub Sastra tersebut mengadakan tradisi pertemuan sastra rutin yami-nabe mereka dengan setiap anggota membacakan karya mereka dengan topik Kematian Shiraishi Itsumi. Nah di sini konflik dimulai, setiap anggota menuliskan pandangan mereka terhadap latar belakang kematian Itsumi dengan setiap orang menyalahkan salah satu anggota lainnya bertanggung jawab atas kematian Itsumi. Format penceritaan yang disajikan menarik, karena berarti kita mendapatkan setiap sudut pandang masing-masing anggota klub sastra. Saya sempat terbawa untuk menebak-nebak mana dari cerita yang berkontradiksi satu sama lain tersebut yang benar dan mana penjahat sesungguhnya. Walaupun setelah pembacaan terakhir, twist sesungguhnya ternyata baru dimulai, kenyataan dibalik pendirian kembali klub sastra oleh Itsumi, latar belakang tiap anggota saat bergabung, serta siapa sesungguhnya yang bertanggung jawab atas kematian Itsumi. Twist-nya rasanya terlalu cepat, seperti dijungkirbalikkan dari fakta yang ada sebelumnya seketika. Tapi tidak masalah. Kemudian rasa-rasanya memang ada orang yang siap membunuh untuk hal-hal yang di luar nalar manusia normal. Mengerikan, tetapi membuat penasaran. 
 Oh ya, hal lain yang menarik adalah tradisi yami-nabe (secara harfiah yami-nabe berarti panci kegelapan). Mungkin permainan ini bisa diterapkan pada kelompok/klub/organisasimu saat acara keakraban atau LDK dan sebagainya. Peraturannya mudah, setiap peserta diwajibkan membawa bahan (sebaiknya yang dapat dimakan) yang dirahasiakan dari peserta lainnya. Semua bahan yang dibawa oleh peserta dimasukkan ke dalam panci berisi air mendidih secara bergantian (bisa sambil melakukan suatu kegiatan)tanpa peserta lain melihat apa yang dimasukkan oleh peserta tersebut. Kemudian semua peserta akan memakan hasil yami-nabe tersebut. Nah, karena saling tidak tahu bahan masing-masing, rasanya mungkin akan menjadi tidak keruan, tetapi jika beruntung mungkin akan enak :P

Tetep ya, endingnya mengejutkan. Walaupun endingnya nggak se-'menakjubkan' bukuHoly Mother cuma tetep aja rasanya mengejutkan. Lebih ke arah ngeri, sih, mengingat tokohnya juga yang ternyata adalah gadis-gadis SMA. Resensi selengkpnya bisa dibaca di MarryingBooks

Walau enjoyable saat dibaca, tapi ini bukan jenis buku yang enak untuk dibaca ulang. 
 Review lengkap: http://lady-storytelling.blogspot.com...

Twist nya cukup berkesan, walaupun sejak awal sudah diantisipasi. 
 Selain itu saya sangat apresiasi sekali usaha penerjemah untuk memberi berbagai informasi tambahan untuk melengkapi cerita. 
 Cerita kurang deskriptif sekali.

Shiraishi Itsumi, si gadis sempurna itu mati 
 Para anggota klub sastra digosipkan sudah membunuh ketua mereka itu 
 Untuk mengenang kematian Itsumi, para anggota klub diundang hadir dan membaca naskah pendek milik mereka. Temanya sudah ditentukan oleh BFF Itsumi, juga wakil ketua klub sastra ini, Sumikawa Sayuri 
 Anggota itu yang terdiri dari Nitani Mirei, Kominami Akane, Diana Detcheva, Koga Sonoko dan Takaoka Shiyo, membacakan cerita pendek versi mereka, dengan tuduhan para pelaku yang berbeda-beda 
 Pembacaan cerita diselingi dengan Yami Nabe 
 Yami Nabe ini menarik sekali untuk diikuti. Jujur, acara yang satu ini bikin imajinasi melayang ke mana-mana 
 Lalu, siapa yang membunuh ketua mereka? 
 Saya agak bingung mereview buku ini 
 Ini bukan jenis buku yang mudah untuk direview, tanpa menebarkan spoiler di sana sini 
 Saya cuma bisa bilang, dari satu cerita ke cerita lainnya, ada banyak ketidak konsistenan 
 Dan itu bikin kita jadi mikir 
 Terus endingnya, biarpun saya agak-agak bisa menebak siapa pelakunya, tetap aja bikin merinding sih 
 Empat bintang 
 Ini pengalaman yang menarik baca J-lit untuk kali pertama

Pertengahan buku udah bisa nebak siapa yang bunuh. 
 Yang paling seru dari buku ini adalah ketika rahasia tiap member klub sastra terkuak. 
 Udah lama nggak baca novel Jepang terbitan haru. Sangat terhibur dengan buku ini.

book_b.title: Safe Haven
book_b.user_review:
Because everybody lies. It's part of living in the society. Don't get me wrong--I think it's necessary. The last thing anyone wants is to live in a society where total honestly prevails. Can you imagine the conversation? You're short and fat, one person might say, and the other might answer, I know, but you smell bad. It just wouldn't work. So people lie by omission all the time. People will tell you most of the story... and I've learned that the part they neglect to tell you is often the most important part. People hide the truth because they're afraid. 
 It doesn't work for me. Don't get me wrong, I'm a big fan of romance, whether it's a movie or book. And most of the time I wouldn't mind a fairy-tale kind of story that has the predictable plot with cheesy lines all the way, unless the girl's a high school student who wants to commit suicide because the boy from the football team wouldn't love her back, most romance works for me. 
 I've heard of Nicholas Sparks so often, but this is the first time I read his book. Based on the reviews of his work, I know that some people really love it while some don't because his writing's so ordinary and too lovey-dovey. I've been prepared by it, but since--as I stated before I'm a fan of romance stories, I don't think it'd be this bad. 
 I was thinking of giving this book a four or even five-star rating until I reached page 371. Everything went downhill since then. I don't like the disclosure at all: I was debating whether to put this book into my "fantasy-myth-creature" section or not. A tiny bit of 'fantasy' that the author put at the ending ruined this whole book. Everything I felt about the characters just melt right at that moment. 
 I actually really enjoyed reading the beginning till the halfway, it was kind of suspense and made my heart and brain worked faster. Although I can easily predict the way the story would end from there--I was thinking that the last page would be their wedding day or the new family's going out at the beach years later or even a hot scene on the bed, I wasn't going to give this book less than three-stars. I feel disappointed and betrayed and I'm not sure if I'm ready for another book of Nicholas Sparks in the near future. Just.. I wish I wouldn't get something like this in any book ever again.

Wow, this book is an exercise in truly trite cliches and sub par writing. WHY does Sparks keep getting published?

http://jocelyns-coffeecorner.blogspot...

Well, it's still not my thing, but this one was worlds better than The Longest Ride. This felt more like a plot driven by believable human beings, as opposed to the banter-driven exercise in the suspension of disbelief that was that rodeo ridiculousness. 
 I'd give it a 3.5, because for a romance novel, it wasn't all that bogged down in romance.

This review and more available at cometgrrl.com. 
 I don't read a lot of chick lit. Well, less than 5 books per year? And since I usually read 50-75 books per year, I'd say that's not a lot, right? And I've never read a Nicholas Sparks novel before. After seeing The Last Song on a flight to Romania a few years ago, I started watching his movies. I think mainly I've been watching on them on airplanes, and really, what else do I have to do for 12 hours on a plane? For some reason, even though I don't read a lot of chit lit novels, I LOVE chick flicks. And so far, I have really enjoyed each of the Nicholas Sparks movies I have seen, with The Last Song being my favorite (c'mon, it's got singing, so of course I love it!). Based on how well I liked the movies, I thought I'd try out one of the books. 
 From what I've read, this book (and the recently released movie, which I have not seen yet) is not your typical Nicholas Sparks story. There is an element of danger in this novel and it deals with somewhat deeper topics than I'd expect in your typical chick lit, and I think, overall, it was really well done. As for the story, I don't want to give anything away -- so go read it! :)

Great book. I've only be able to read half of one of Nicholas Sparks books. There's all so sad and depressing. (The time travelers Wife made me cry for days!). After seeing the trailer for the movie I went and downloaded the book. Glad I did. There was a kind of mystery to it, that I loved. The ending was sad and made to tear up (a lot) but I couldn't put the book down! 24hours and I was done.
Really liked this book. Although I didn't get how Joe turned out to be unreal. Great novel by Sparks, as always!
