reference_books.title: A Thousand Pieces of You (Firebird, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I was not expecting to much, I read the blurb and thought sounds interesting, but what the blurb doesn't tell you this is great read. 
 Maguerita Caine loves her family she will do everything to get revenge after Paul who she thought was her friend killed that her father. 
 Her parents discovered the Firebird which allows people to jump in parallel universes, she will follow Paul straight in to hell if she has to, but she will catch him. 
 Together with Theo the follow Paul trough different worlds, where she meets her family again and again in alternate lives and Paul to. But the thing is Paul was always nice to her and the alternate Paul loves her and she loves him. 
 Get ready for a roller-coaster ride this book was action packed, has great characters, good world building and off course a heartbreaking love story as well.

book_a.title: Wild Awake
book_a.user_review:
3.5 stars this was a nice refreshing and a little bit crazy read. 
 Kiri get's a call one day when her parents are off cruising the Caribbean, some one calls hers telling to come and get her sisters stuff. Who happens to be dead for 5 years. So she decided to go, but things turn out a lot different than picking up stuff and Kiri meets Skunk a big beefy guy. 
 When Kiri founds out what really happened to her sister she losses it, she crumbles and stops sleeping. The writer did an excellent job with the story because I can actually feel Kiri becoming lucid. I liked Skunk to but I didn't like the open ending, I wanted to know how the story ended. Did they stay together, did her parents finally talked to her, did she get treatment. Why were her parents so strange? What happened with the piano performance? Is there mental illness in her family? 
 Overall an very entertaining read.

sample_reviews.review_text:
I really don't get why people like this book. I felt like I was going crazy reading it! 
 Rating: 0/10 
 Full review at Unraveling Books
I don't know how I feel... review to come.

This was a fast paced story and there where things I liked about it, and things I did NOT like about it. 
 The protagonist, Kiri Byrd, is a teen girl, going through teen stuff. 
 Her perspective of this world, is shattered once her parents go on holiday and leave her in charge: to look after herself. However, she receives a phone call one night which causes her to tear off into the night, without regard to her safety. 
 She finds out the story behind her sisters murder 7 years ago and her world begins to crumble. 
 What unfolds from this journey is cause for alarm, as she realises her stupidity. Unfortunately for her she cannot let it go and so continues into many 'first,' and even mental illness. The pace of the story speeds up even more through her mind and through her voice - Smith, has written this pace very well. 
 During the story there were times I liked her character, and times I hated her, not her personally, but her decisions she makes and the things she does. 
 Her life in nigh on the verge of stardom, and also destruction. 
 Some of the situations were predictable, sort of, but I predicted the ending wrongly. In fact the end, isn't really the end. it is sort of a new beginning, of which she is very lucky to have the chance at. 
 Great read, but a very dark story: in fact, I'm not sure the target age for this story is appropriate at times.

This book should be part of the advocacy campaign for child welfare laws. Seriously. What kind of parents, after losing one daughter to a brutal murder, leaves their only remaining daughter alone for SIX ENTIRE WEEKS so they can go on a romantic vacation for two? 
 Ones who should not ever be allowed to parent, that's who. 
 I'll admit, this book...it riveted me. Because it was crazy. Full-on batshit. And don't get me wrong, I'm not being insensitive to those with mental health problems, trust me. I understand it better than you will ever know, but I'm not sure I get the point of writing about it in this way. If anything, I think it's the author here who's been insensitive. Don't tackle a subject like this if you're not going to do it right! Where's the lesson here? Where is the resolution? What did this book teach me? Nothing, other than that this author has the ability to mimic a pretty well detailed psychotic episode on paper, and to demonstrate the ways in which to grind up a nug and pack a bowl. 
 I'm baffled as to how this was bought and is now being marketed as a young adult novel, because I can tell you right now, if I had a young adult...I would never, ever allow him or her to read this. This book isn't suitable for children with impressionable minds who might think Kiri's summer adventures are something to mimic. Like riding a bicycle into downtown to meet some sketchy guy after dark. Like going into said strange guys sketchy apartment building even after being warned that it could be a scam. Like going home with someone she doesn't know who's offered to fix her bike. Like accepting drugs from strangers! 
 I'm cringing at my own words right now, because I feel like I sound like one of those old crotchety ladies who shakes their fingers at anything fun, but really. I dare you to read this and then come back and tell me you don't agree with what I'm saying. And if you don't, I'd like to hear why, maybe you can enlighten me on something I missed.

What was the purpose to this book? What was it about? Because everything was a mess, much like the protagonist. 
 I cannot believe the book ended where it had ended - without giving us any sense of closure. Tying any of those story arcs up would've upped this book at least by two stars for me. But we go through all that struggle of reading mostly redundant scenes about the protagonist reeling out of control without that being dealt with in any way. 
 And nothing bothers me more than music elitists. When you make fun of cover bands, you do realise that the pieces that you're playing by Bach and Beethoven are basically covers. Way to be a hypocrite. Maybe it's another issue about the protagonist that isn't addressed, but that lady bitches about other musicians throughout the book like it's no one's business. 
 I also found it hard to like any of the characters in the book, and that usually doesn't work for me when I read a book. 
 I do have high praise for the author though, because the writing was great. I could feel myself travelling downward along with the protagonist and her trips. 
 In all its demented and chaotic glory, I would've enjoyed this so much more if at least one of the arcs had been tied up properly.

Two stars because honestly, this is just not my type of book. I'm not giving it a low rating because it is poorly-written (it is beautifully written); I'm not giving it a low rating because I think it's marketed to the wrong demographic (young adults, believe it or not, are capable of handling a story like this in a detached, don't-try-this-at-home manner. They're not going to look at Kiri's so-called "adventures" and think OH THAT LOOKS LIKE FUN. Nothing about Wild Awake is fun. Nothing.); I'm not giving it a low rating because the parents are so unbelievably absent (yeah, bad parents happen in real life, too, so forgive me if I don't take away stars because they happened in this book). 
 I am giving it a low rating because I never got attached to the characters. Because I was unsettled by Kiri's personality, as well as the inconsistency between her narrative tone and the tone of the book itself. Because I'm not sure it handled the topic of mental illness all that well. Because I wasn't convinced by the romance, and Kiri's grand statements about how hopelessly in love she and Skunk are-- all while still comparing him to large, wild animals in her head ("love-bison"? "Brontosaurus of love"? Really? I get it. He's not a small dude. The elephant tranquilizers kind of drove that point home)-- made me uncomfortable. 
 Several times while reading this book, I wanted to be reading something else. Anything else. Now, tell me if I'm wrong, but I'm pretty sure that's not supposed to happen. I skipped a giant chunk toward the end and didn't feel like I had missed anything important, because the entire book is a lot of the same over and over: Kiri gets drunk, Kiri gets high, Kiri cries and thinks about the injustice her family has wrought upon her, Kiri suddenly feels good and inspired and like everything is fine, someone tells Kiri she is crazy, Kiri is sad and thinks about her sister, Kiri does something reckless, etc. Repeat. Character development? Look elsewhere. You might say that she learned her lesson toward the end and actually started growing up, but if you look closely you'll notice that the same thing happened several times already. Why should I believe that this mature perspective will last any longer than it did the last time she decided to change her ways?

When I first read about Wild Awake I was super excited to read it. The cover looked gorgeous and the synopsis sounded different and interesting. While I did enjoy my reading experience, I was never really as blown away as others were. 
 One thing I can completely agree with others about is Hilary T. Smith's writing. Like Kiri throughout most of the book, the writing is very much strange but mesmerizing. It fits into the stream of consciousness type of writing, which I found really worked with Kiri considering her state of mind for most of the book. 
 While some people might be uncomfortable with the explicit use of drugs in this book, or any other book, I'm not. Whether you like it or not, drugs are used everyday by so many people, young and old, and I didn't find that it detracted from the characters or the situations at all. Due to recent events and where her head was at at that point, I found it understandable why she holed herself up with drugs and music. She needed comfort and a safe place and she found it there. 
 While I really wanted to love this book more, I just wasn't pushed to that point. But that's okay because I still found it enjoyable. Like I said before the writing was amazing, the romance between Kiri and Skunk was sweet and unpredictable, and the narration was often witty and funny. Definitely worth a shot if you're looking for a different type of contemporary!

SOME SPOILERS. You have been warned! 
 I really liked "Wild Awake"...and the fact that it's a debut book surprised me a little. The narrator Kiri is very much in her own head for a lot of the book, so much of what's happening comes from her POV which is interesting. Even as things start to spiral for her, she becomes increasingly obsessed with what happened to her older sister (whom she idolized) Sukey: causing her to smoke a lot of pot, and take some risky night-time bike rides, among other things. While the adults in her life are worried about this Risky Behavior (Kiri has 'unsubscribed' to sleep, and instead spends her nights smoking/being destructive to the yard/with her friend Skunk) Kiri describes her life as simply being really, extra, super awake: "wild awake". I really loved the writing in this book. It's poetic and artsy without being too out there, even though Kiri is kind of wacko. I found myself wondering whether or not she was high as a kite, many times, but I do believe she only took two drugs throughout the book...she was just so awake and so chattery, it was hard to tell. (Or maybe she was just so hopped up about her sister, she was "high on life" as they say. But I have a sneaking suspicion that she was stoned for like, 80% of the time, and I just went with it. 
 The amount of pot she smokes throughout the story actually struck me as a bit implausible, but I let it slide, anyway. Kiri seems an unstable kind of person. I do not believe that the majority of 17 yr olds smoke THAT much pot on a daily basis (I've never tried the stuff, but I'm also the kind of person who watches Netflix pretty much all weekend, when given the chance) but all in all, I wasn't too bothered by it. At least Kiri wasn't finding solace in (what I refer to as) the Hardcore Stuff-cocaine, heroin, etc, or I would've put the book down immediately. (Books involving a lot of drugs other than cigarettes or pot is a turn off for me.) 
 Hilary T Smith is one to watch, and I would definitely consider reading any of her other books...4 stars for her!

 It is obviously a metaphor for human society and the "Beast" enclosed within us with a patina of civilization that is ever so fragile. F.A. Hayek, in his treatise, "The Constitution of Liberty," states that when individual liberty is forsaken the only possible results are anarchy or dictatorship. In this extraordinary novel, we have both: Jack is the narcissistic dictator that rules by force and eventually by terror and torture to ensure obedience. 
 Ralph (I assume pronounced "Rafe", since all the children are British--perhaps considered the most civilized and civilizing nation)represents civilization, representative government, reason, etc. Without the civilizing force of society, brute force in the form of Jack banishes him, and with him, rationality and humanity. The "id," the "heart of darkness," and bestiality are the inevitable result. 
 We also have "Piggy" the scientist and rationalist advisor to Ralph and Simon, who I see as the philosopher who in Plato's Allegory of the Sun sees reality, where "truth and beauty shine resplendent." As a consequence of being the one being who can bring down Jack by identifying the "Beast" as really a man (and, consequently, the real Beast hiding in all of us beneath a veneer of civilization) he is therefore slaughtered. 
 Although there were parts that seemed a little slow, the payoff came only as a result of those parts and was overwhelming for me. 
 ...A truly extraordinary piece.

reference_books.title: Thinking, Fast and Slow
reference_books.review_text:
I picked up this book on the recommendation of another writer, and I'm very glad I did. This is hardly the kind of book I would read (I spent much of college hoping no one would tell me I had to take math or physics), but the author is a brilliant teacher if this book is any indication. Daniel Kahneman won the Nobel Prize for economics, and takes us through the process of learning to recognize how we think and how statistics and economic theory will help us improve our thinking. (God knows mine could use some help.) 
 The author proposes two thinking systems, if you will. System I is responsible for all those wonderful intuitions that we heavily rely on to get us through challenging times. It produces decisions, ideas, reactions and answers to questions rapidly, leaving us emotionally satisfied. "It felt right. I had this gut feeling. . ." System 2 is slower because it is analyzing the question and the data presented, and working out a solution. System 2 is math or logic--it is thinking hard. (System 1 is thinking easy.) 
 This is a fascinating look at how our mind tricks us into being illogical, non-rational, and lazy. (And we all are much of the time.) The author examines heuristics and biases, our various illusions, and the way we make choices. Although I had to work hard sometimes after the first half to keep up with discussion about a field I never studied, the author makes this material so fresh and interesting that I refused to quit. I have no doubt that those within the fields of statistics, economics, logic, psychology, and philosophy would find much to debate here, but for a reader who was blissfully unaware of her ignorance, enlightenment has been both reasonably painless and exciting.

reference_books.title: The Woman Upstairs
reference_books.review_text:
I thought about this book a lot while I was reading it, instead of sinking into the story and letting it carry me along. I had heard other readers and reviewers comment about their feelings about the main character, and I recognized immediately what they were talking about. My rating of this book reflects my respect for what the author attempted and achieved, but not positive feelings for the story. 
 Nora Eldridge is a third-grade school teacher who lives alone, has no man in her life, and thinks of herself as the woman upstairs, a stock character who lives quietly out of sight and never makes trouble for anyone, the reliable, uninteresting nondescript woman we all fail to acknowledge. Into her world comes Reza Shahid, a new student in Cambridge for a year while his father enjoys a visiting fellowship and his mother, Sirena, an artist, tries to work on her art away from her friends and studio in Paris. Nora falls in love with Reza, a beautiful exotic little boy that she seems to have a special affinity for. Sirena invites her to share a studio space, and Nora feels validated as an artist, a part of herself she had set aside and essentially given up on. Over the weeks of the beginning of the school term, Nora is drawn closer and closer to the Shahid family, enjoying family dinners and long talks with the father, Skandar, when he walks her home. There are numerous references to literary works--Ibsen's "Doll House," a short story by Chekhov, and Ralph Ellison's "The Invisible Man," are the most obvious. 
 Nora makes clear at the outset that she is angry, enraged at the world, caught in the Fun House that is life. She shares her story as though she were an older woman who has missed out on life, is trapped in a dead-end job and caring for elders, and finds little joy in the world. But this woman is only in her early forties, and has almost no demands on her life other than a job. Her widowed father needs minimal care, and her best friend gives her sensible and kind advice. Nora is also apparently unique in her generation for having no online presence, no cyber friends or connections. Nora as a character evokes images of single women in the 1950s, not the 2010s. Her choices for her art project, building dioramas, are also from an earlier time--Emily Dickinson, Alice Neel, Virginia Woolf, and Edie Sedgwick. 
 Everything in the story shouts art and the artist's life, and asks where is the boundary between artist and parent, art and friendship, art and meaning, art and understanding. 
 The ambivalence I feel is between admiration for the sheer skill required to create and maintain the character of Nora and my disappointment at the ending, where, on reflection, I expected more. I cannot say that the ending seems consistent with Nora's character, nor inconsistent; it seemed convenient. End the story with a solid punch. For me, in the end the story seemed more clever than edifying.

reference_books.title: The Giver (The Giver, #1)
reference_books.review_text: I picked up this book from a Little Free Library, and otherwise would not have encountered it. This is the story of a young boy in a dystopian community that is chosen to be the receiver of memories. In a world that is cleansed of all extremes, in weather, human relationships, etc., one person must hold the memories of the way life had been for centuries, before the community opted for "sameness." The Giver is the current Receiver, who must pass on his memories to a younger member, Jonas. Unfortunately, with experience, in this case experience of memories, comes questioning and dissatisfaction and wonder and curiosity. Jonas and the Giver work to resolve Jonas's growing unsettledness as he learns more through memories. The book raises numerous questions about quality of life, and how that is defined.

reference_books.title: The Spy Who Came In from the Cold
reference_books.review_text:
My family talked about this book for years, and I came away thinking I had read it. But I began to wonder if I had. It's interesting to read this well-known book after the spy and thriller genre have developed so much. 
 Leamas runs the network in Berlin, and the story opens with an agent being killed while trying to cross from East to West. Leamas returns to London, having lost basically his entire network of agents, and is headed for retirement. He and his superiors come up with a plan to trap his nemesis, Mundt, which will be Leamas's last job. Leamas is fired ostensibly, gets a job, and falls in love with a young woman, which is not part of the plan. 
 The plan works, Leamas is picked up and taken to East Germany, and the plan for implicating Mundt in complicity with the West is set in motion. For those who haven't read it, I'll stop here, but I will say that the story unrolls surprise after surprise, right until the end. 
 This book was riveting in the 1960s when it was first published, and it still is. There are differences between the spy/thriller novel of the 1960s and today. The middle part of the book felt very "talky," and the end also became "talky" as Leamas explained to another what had happened. I didn't feel the explanation was necessary, but I can see that it would be welcomed by some readers. 
 The ending is unsettling because it is honest, and le Carre didn't alter the story to please readers. It's hard to know if the ending should have been kinder or harder, but the entire story is memorable for the view into a world of people supposedly working for high principles with no illusions about what will succeed and what will fail. The ends and the means are not the same in this book.

book_a.title: Stasiland: Stories from Behind the Berlin Wall
book_a.user_review:
I picked up this book thinking it was a collection of stories that might be as good as the story behind the movie THE LIVES OF OTHERS. When I realized it was memoir/report about what life had been like before the wall fell, I was even more interested. Funder meets various people in East Berlin and other cities that were part of the GDR, including members of the Stasi, and interviews them. She also visits one of the prisons, and sees the torture cells. It's very chilling. There is nothing in crime fiction that comes close to the real terror that the Stasi inflicted on people. 
 When I finished the book I thought about the writing. Each sentence is perfectly chiseled. She is never literary, searching for similes or turns of phrase to change the nature of the story. It's a remarkable book and I don't think I'll ever forget it. One of the most redeeming passages was a phone call with a woman who left Germany for San Francisco and was somewhat amazed that people talked all the time about what had happened to them and how they were overcoming it. After living under the Stasi and undergoing some horrendous experiences, she had found a place to recover her life.

This book was invaluable on a recent trip to Berlin, which I'd last visited before the Wall came down in 1988. The GDR is still recent history and yet we hear little about it, or how its legacy is affecting lives in today's united Germany. Acting on her hunch that important stories were in danger of being lost, Funder does much to remedy this gap in understanding, telling the stories of both Stasis officials and the casualties of the regime in a very, human readable way.

book_b.title: The Odds: A Love Story
book_b.user_review:
This is a slight (in the sense of short and easy story) book covering a last desperate weekend for Art and Marion as they celebrate their thirtieth reunion and try to win enough money in a casino at Niagara Falls to stave off foreclosure and bankruptcy. Their marriage hasn't been successful, and each spouse ruminates on a past indiscretion that could have sunk the marriage years ago but didn't. The setting includes a suite that contrasts only in opulence with the mundane, kitschy pastimes enjoyed by almost all visitors to the Falls. Art wants to relive the sparkle and promise of their honeymoon and win back the woman he's wronged in several ways, and Marion isn't sure where she wants to drift to. 
 The two middle-class and middle-aged Americans are holding on by their fingernails. Through their eyes we get a closer look at the casino world from those who know it only peripherally. The high-stakes rooms are just as fake as the museums the couple take in over the weekend, and gambling even on this level seems pedestrian. By the end of the weekend, however, Art and Marian are better able to assess what they do and do not have.

sample_reviews.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 I had some issues with this book. 
 1. The main characters, Art and Marion, seem to think that winning a huge amount of money will fix their marriage. 
 2. Many couples divorce because of finances, and this book reinforces the thought that a successful marriage is linked to how much money you have. 
 3. The affairs were dim, and only offered a small glimpse of what they were missing emotionally from the marriage. 
 4. Each chapter started off with a fact about the odds of something happening. These were spoilers for the chapter to come. 
 5. When their daughter Emma called about her proposal, Art and Marion were happy but both were too preoccupied with their own state of affairs to truly cherish the moment. What kind of parenting message is this? 
 6. Miscommunication is a bigger problem than finances, and although the miscommunication was clear between the characters, it just didn't get resolved. Yeah, they win big at the end but they still don't know how to talk to each other. 
 7. The characters both got the shits from eating bad seafood. Is this a metaphor I missed? They cared for each other when it happened, but other than that I didn't really see the significance. 
 I did like the first couple of chapters because the writing really gave a sense of longing and it was emotional. But as the story progressed, I just lost interest and found myself disagreeing more than emphasizing.

A brief character sketch-- felt like a short story. The two were full of the inner dialogue that made their relationship so real and believable, though there's not a lot of story going on. Food for thought, though I'm not sure I liked it--maybe even in large part because of the last line. I don't think this book should try to summarize itself so glibly. Much of the study is very heartfelt, but I felt the author trying very hard, too.
I'd give it 3.5 stars, not my fave of his, but not bad either. I do want to read Last Night At the Lobster again now.

MY REVIEW: 
 Penguin Books|September 25, 2012|Trade Paperback|ISBN: 978-0-14-312227-2 
 "Stewart O'Nan's thirteenth novel is another wildly original, bittersweet gem like his celebrated Last Night at the Lobster. 
 Valentine's weekend, Art and Marion Fowler flee their Cleveland suburb for Niagara Falls, desperate to recoup their losses. Jobless, with their home approaching foreclosure and their marriage on the brink of collapse, Art and Marion liquidate their savings account and book a bridal suite at the Falls ritziest casino for a second honeymoon. While they sightsee like tourists during the day, at night they risk it all at the roulette wheel to fix their finances - and save their marriage. A tender yet honest exploration of faith, forgiveness, and last chances. THE ODDS is a reminder that love, like life, is always a gamble." 
 According to the above synopsis of THE ODDS from the Chapters website, the book sounds like an interesting read. However, quite the opposite is true. I just couldn't get into this story at all. I found is painfully boring and slow with no excitement or anything to even entince me to try to keep reading further. I did give it a good try and perservered through the first five chapters but just couldn't push myself any further. I would not recommend this book to anyone.

Stewart O'Nan seems to be one of those uniquely talented writers that never has a blockbuster. I have read several of his books and I think I might know why. He is undeniably a very talented writer and I always enjoy his books... to a point. Every book of his that I have read has always been missing something. Sometimes it's better character development, sometimes a better plot. His novels always JUST seem to miss the mark. In this novel I was really enjoying the story and was really thinking this was the best O'Nan yet... until I reached the end. The characters, while not particularly likable, were interesting. The plot had huge holes in it, a device frequently used by O'Nan, seemingly to creat intrigue,but was still interesting. O'Nan tends to focus on the mundane and leave the bigger picture a little blurry. Even that didn't bother me so much. It was the ending that killed the whole book for me. It was abrupt and jarring. His last line, an attempt to sound profound, came off as trite to me. I was just beginning to connect with the characters and the difficult decisions that had led them to Niagra Falls and their trying to save themselves, when O'Nan ended the book. His cutting the reader off from the "rest of the story" left me feeling like the book was unfinished. Sadly I cannot recommend this one.

This book did a nice job developing its characters and setting, which was especially amusing to me while I was on vacation with my husband. It was a four-star read until I got to the two-star final pages. While the roulette metaphor mostly worked, it became all too obvious and trite in the end. Meh.
Definitely not one of my favorite reads.
I did enjoy learning about Niagara Falls. I had no idea it was such a tourist destination. I did enjoy the look into a failing relationship.

Not sure what to make of this one. A married couple are simultaneously let go of their jobs. After 30 years of comfortable middle-class existence supported by two incomes. They are now unemployed, with a large second mortgage, on the verge of foreclosure, bankruptcy and divorce. They make this strange pack to go to their honeymoon gambling hotel in Canada and decide to roll the dice to save their marriage and their finances. The story moves back and forth in time letting the reader know what is going on in their heads, including the grudges they have harbored against each other. The things each has done and regretted. The characters felt real and I liked them. The plot and ending were too unrealistic for me to buy.

Art and Marion are on the brink of bankruptcy and divorce when they decide to risk everything on a second honeymoon to Niagra Falls. It's a very simple story, examining in brief the reasons their marriage and finances have crumbled as they spend their days sightseeing and their evenings at the roulette wheel. The novel is short, under 200 pages, but it doesn't feel like a rushed job. Instead, it feels like a master storyteller exerting control. If O'Nan had kept the story going, he'd almost certainly have ruined it. The beauty here isn't in the complexity of the story, but instead in O'Nan's gift for capturing the mundane and the everyday in language that is fluid and lovely without outgrowing itself.

sample_reviews.review_text: I was looking forward to reading this, but I just didn't 'get it' - I am usually a fan of short story collections. I found this contained too strained of a narrative most of the time to continue. I was a little bored & a little perturbed with the lack of quotation marks for conversations.

Grrr. I am conflicted in my review of this book. I wanted to like it. And the blurbs on the back from some top-notch writers suggests that maybe I'm just "missing something" or that I'm not deep enough or sharp enough or abstract-thinking enough! Not true. But darn it all I just DISLIKED every one of the characters in this book. 
 I mean, every single one of them was a fringe-of-society weirdo. Sure, one can write about weirdos and try to give meaning and justification to their lives but there was something so off-putting about these characters. One can enjoy a good story about a loser but an entire book of stories about losers gets a little nauseous. I certainly never felt closer to any of these characters by being able to see into their inner lives. In fact I was just more repelled. "It Chooses You" was a lot better because it was about real people. Somehow that made a difference with me. 
 Nobody in this book seems to do much either. They always seem to be sitting on the patio or standing on the sidewalk or lying on the floor of their bedrooms looking at dust-bunnies under the bed or sitting on the couch slowly going through the want ads. Only the woman in the last story seemed slightly interesting. But again she was just another loser that let people take advantage of her, for her entire life. 
 p.s. Miranda July should read Tenth of December and learn how to actually write a story.

sample_reviews.review_text: Trying to decided whether I enjoyed Crime and Punishment or The Brothers Karamazov more!

Holy crap....I thought Crime and Punishment was a tough read, but at least there was an interesting story with a deep psychological twist. I have been looking forward to this one for a long time, and now I am just disappointed. I suppose in literary snob circles, folks like to sit around and analyze each book and chapter of this incredibly long and boring tome. Not me, I am at a point in my life where I like a good story that tracks along at a decent pace. This is a book where literally nothing happens for 1000 pages. I tried....I failed...I need some Travis McGee style misogynistic fluff to get me over this.

Unexceptional story line, but great characters and theological asides. This is the only book I've ever read that was actually able to pull off the "I'll tell you how it'll end and then try to make you believe that something different from what I've said would happen will happen" device.

Today was a day many months in the making: when I finally finished what I fully expect to be the last Russian book I ever read. 
 I feel like I have given Russian lit an honest try. I self-assigned Anna Karenina first, and quickly came to the conclusion that clawing my eyeballs out would have hurt less. But after a few years, I decided that I had probably been too young to properly understand it (I was in junior high), so I tried again with Crime Punishment, figuring that in my role in dealing with the law would make this a valuable read. But once again, I was looking for an anvil to fall on my head and shorten my misery. But I decided that third time pays for all, and I tried Dostoevsky's class about faith, suffering, and family. 
 Yeah. Hated this too. 
 Now, I have to say that some of the fault might be mine. I read it over a series of months, with long periods in between, so by the time I reached the end I really didn't remember what happened at the beginning. I struggled with keeping the characters straight, especially since I don't especially understand Russian naming systems. I was still confusing the three brothers and their various nicknames almost halfway through the book. I really could not understand a lot of the cultural background, and I think that having some details would have provided me the structure to understand the story better. I could sense brilliance just below the surface, but I couldn't access it or understand it. Yes, I'm apparently a plebe. I did enjoy the courtroom scenes at the very end, especially the two sides' closing arguments, but other than that all I could think was "WHEN will this be done?" I think I have made an honest effort, but I also think that this will be the last piece of Russian lit I read again, at least without some help.

Okay, so, I am biased. I generally dislike Russian lit; I particularly dislike Dostoevsky. I dislike Dostoevsky more now than I did before reading this. I will concede that the novel, particularly the last 150 pages has serious literary heft and some crazily beautiful philosophy. This does not, however, make The Brothers Karamazov an enjoyable read. I know that I sound decidedly lazy when I say this, but it's just so darned long! This book could easily have been 300 pages shorter with very little sacrificed. Overall, I can't say it's something I would read again.

This is, in my opinion, his best book. I think it's much better than Crime and Punishment. Russian literature has always captivated me and Dostoyevsky does a fantastic job with the character development in this novel.
I read this in H.S. as part of my AP English class. Quite possibly the WORST book I've ever read.
Disappointing. Interminable dialogues that went on for pages and said nothing. Characters too unsympathetic. Incongruous setting for the discussion of supposedly lofty issues. I was expecting more.

This one turned out to be too difficult for me to get into. I got until page 140 and then I gave up. It's a tough storyline, slow, difficult to grasp. At page 140 I still did not understand what the individual characters were about. Also, Dostoyevsky uses multiple names for single characters, which makes it difficult to understand who in fact he is talking about. I gave it a try, but the 19th century writers are not for me I guess.

I read about 3 translations of this book (I say about because I stopped reading the others when I found this one) and this is by far the best translation. I don't know about accurate, I'm still in elementary Russian, but this is just a well written translation.

reference_books.title: Dark Heir (Jane Yellowrock, #9)
reference_books.review_text:
I received an ARC via blog tour in exchange for an honest review 
 Faith Hunter delivers another stellar installment of the Jane Yellowrock series (one of my all-time faves) with DARK HEIR! While Jane kicks ass in the fighting scenes, it's her range of emotion that truly comes through the page. Humor, love, anger, remorse, insecurity, and more draw you in and make Jane and her fellow characters all that more real. 
 I loved that DARK HEIR circles back to plot lines that occurred early in the series, as well as, continues to move towards the upcoming confrontation with the European vamps. It enriches the world...all the while proving that vampires are very tricksy creatures...setting events into motion years (and years) in the past. 
 Another love? The Younger brothers! Those guys absolutely rock!!!! They are 100% there for Jane and after so long of being let down by people she loves, it's wonderful to see that there are people who will always have her back and give her the family she deserves. 
 As for Jane's love life? She's doing pretty good on that front. There's a little tiny interaction with Ricky Bo...but it's quick...which frankly is a bit more than I think Jane ever needs to give him! She's much better off with Bruiser! As for Bruiser...we don't get to spend a lot of time with him, but the time we do? *Sigh* Keep it up big guy! 
 Another slight disappointment? Not as much Beast time. I love the interactions between Jane and Beast and especially when we get Beast's POV. While there is some in DARK HEIR, there's not as much as you can find in previous books. The two are more integrated now which is pretty cool, but I love seeing the world through Beast's eyes. 
 Overall, DARK HEIR is a MUST READ so make sure it's on your MUST BUY list come April 7th!

reference_books.title: Death's Rival (Jane Yellowrock, #5)
reference_books.review_text:
Wow! Death's Rival starts off strong and doesn't let up. Jane faces betrayals, demons from her own forgotten past, and is thrust into the heart of war between two master vampires. 
 Jane is once again working for Leo Pellisier (Master of the City of New Orleans and the Southeast US) and as a plague spreads through the vampire world, Leo sends his self-proclaimed Enforcer out to find answers. As Jane investigates, threads tie back to events that occurred in Ashville in book 4, Raven Cursed, and even back further into the history of skinwalkers. All the while, Jane is also trying to uncover who might be the mole in Leo's organization. 
 As much as I enjoy the fast-pace of Death's Rival, I'm truely enjoying seeing how much Jane has grown throughout the series. Not only is she learning more about her early years and actions, she's coming to grips with how her life continues to evolve from a penniless vampire hunter to the enforcer of a powerful and wealthy vampire. 
 You could read Death's Rival as a stand alone, but I recommend the entire series as you'll get more of the characters' motivations and overall series arc. I'm looking forward to Blood Trade coming out in April 2013.

sample_reviews.review_text: I tried and tried, but just could not get into this book.

Nothing against the book, if I was younger I suppose I would enjoy it more...... just a wee bit tired of reading about teeny-boppers. Life isn't exciting only when you are that young...... makes.me.feel.OLD.

Violet Lee finds herself a witness to a massacre and then kidnapped by a group claiming to be vampires. They give her a choice to become a vampire or to stay as their guest (kidnap victim) until she agrees to become a vampire. Violet is about to find out that the world is much more then what she thought it was. 
 I realize that this was written by a young person and is quite an achievement. However, if this is aimed at young people then it sends some pretty messed up messages about what is acceptable relationship behaviour and what is forgivable. I also find the blurb on the front misleading "The sexiest romance you'll read this year." Umm, no it wasn't, not by a long shot. I'm not going to tear this book to shreds, though I am sure other people will do it for me. Let me just say that it did get better towards the end of the book but then again that wasn't hard.

I blame Twilight for the spawn of a whole genre of books like THIS; 
 "Dinner With a Vampire" 
 KILL IT! KILL IT WITH FIRE! 
 This book is AWFUL. The blurb sounded promising, it gave the impression of a dark, alternate world that a young girl finds herself trapped in - DO NOT BE FOOLED. It is the latest in Vampire fiction, and (dare I say it?) The worst one yet. The protagonist is a pathetic girl who falls for the Vampire "Prince" who captures her. 
 What the male lead IS NOT: 
 - Sexy.....no, no, no....no. 
 - Charming. (Far from it, he threatens to RAPE her - yeah because that's totally swoon-worthy and not a reason to stitch up your own vajajay.) 
 - Mysterious (She hears him have sex with other vampires on a frequent basis, kind of takes the "mystery" out of him.) 
 - Funny -_- 
 What the female lead IS NOT: 
 - Interesting (She gives Bella Swan a run for her money in the whining department.) 
 - Intelligent (If she were intelligent she would know that threatening RAPE is not a form of foreplay!) 
 - Funny -_- 
 I genuinely think the author was high when she was writing this. 
 This book ticks off every mind-numbing cliche and after finishing the first 400 pages I just couldn't bring myself to drag myself through the last 100. At least this way I can convince myself that the "heroine" died tragically while her love-interest was trapped in his own bondage. Far more satisfying. 
 Awful. Just truly, truly awful. 
 EDIT!! 
 I just found out that the author began writing and posting this novel at fifteen before publishing it three years later. For a fifteen year old the writing shows a lot of promise, that being said after accepting a publishing deal she should have fine-tuned her book A LOT. I still don't think that the threat of rape should be thrown around so lightly in a YA novel and generally this new information doesn't change my opinion all that much.

Ultimately, it was just okay. Lots of descriptive writing as far as world-building, but not much in the explanation of the rules of the world-building. The heroine cried, a lot, and the hero was an ass. Mostly, the story just rambled along, seemingly going nowhere, and then just kind of...ended. Glad I only spent $2.99 on the ebook.

This is why.

But she is found out on a secret, that her dad killed his mom NOT HER BUT HER DAD. anyway they drag her by the head of hair outside across gravel, place a knife at her throat and decide to kill her. Kaspar all this time is looking at her as she cries but o no he is way to angry to help her. So he walks away to let her die. But a different guy saves her. Anyway it gets worse.

 AHHHHHH HE WAS PREPARED TO LET HER DIE, AND SHE BECAME A DOOR MAT. I JUST COULDN'T READ ANYMORE.

This book gives me the confidence that if it - with all its blatant grammatical errors and inconsistent characterisations and more-than-cliche plot development - can get published, then damn it all, my books will surely get published too one day.

Could not get into this - loved the premise, loved the cover (!), not so much the actual storytelling. I tried twice, about a month apart, got to chapter 8 and gave it up. These may just be style issues but.... here's my concerns, you decide if they do or don't bother you. 
 Continuity - Brooke and her I-don't-even-know-what-to-call-him guy, Sean, are in a muddle. This is the very beginning of the book, so I'm not spoiling things, after all, she has to move on from him if she & Jett are going to work. Anyway, she seems to really not understand how Sean sees the relationship even though she describes it early in - they are not exclusive, yet the dynamic plays out as if she thinks they are. I could've looked past this but the other issues? 
 Drinking - the first seven chapters include two nights of such high alcohol intake that our heroine, Brooke, doesn't remember what happened and she wakes up having spent the night with Jett both times. This is after she met him at a business meeting set in a strip club. I'm not a prude (at all, see my other reviews) but these plot devices were so far beyond logical that I couldn't stick with it. There are other, even more unlikely business details that defied belief. 
 Brooke and her roommate, Sylvie, come across as unlikeably shallow. Brooke talks about being professional and yet, she's not. (Showing up hungover for work, showing up for her first day on a new job....). 
 I try to write from the positive but sometimes a book just doesn't work for me. Authors work hard to pull a story together and I'm respectful of the effort they put into their storytelling.

T.E.R.R.I.B.L.E!!! I'm convinced that the high rating on this book must be from the author and her friends, because this book isn't just a little bit terrible, it's incredibly terrible. I'm being generous when I say the characters are wildly erratic, illogical and juvenile. They are poorly developed and hard to believe. There are so many errors in the book, like the girls eyes are first hazel and then brown. The type of car she drives changes, first Chevy and then it's suddenly an old Volvo. There are tons of things like this. And then, the worst part is the insane story line. Spoiler alert, not that it should matter: A super smart, very successful business man tries to ensnare the woman thru lust or love because he wants to take and/or buy her inheritance but he doesn't think thru what will happen when she inevitably finds out she's inheriting the piece of property he's been trying to acquire for 10 years and that he's willing to overpay extravagantly to acquire. I mean WTF?!? Really!?! 
 The author had the makings of a really cool plot and then she totally butchered every aspect of the book. Do not waste your time or money.

I started reading this book b/c I needed something light after I finished The Fault in our Stars. This is so light, you'd have to be brain dead to enjoy it. I don't even know where to begin. 
 First, our idiot protagonist has a "business" meeting with an executive of a TOP COMPANY in a strip club. If you can muddle through that...the executive pretends to be someone else, instead of himself. And is wearing jeans. Assuming I can use a brain cell to believe for a second that an actual business meeting...for a REAL ESTATE company...is occurring in a strip club, there's no chance that an exec would show up in jeans. Or pretend to be someone else. And she's chugging margaritas while waiting for him. Oh-Kay. And that's just the first chapter, folks. 
 It gets worse from there. Our heroine says repeatedly that she never gets drunk after: A. Telling us multiple times that she and her drunk whore of a roommate are regulars at a bar down the street; B. Getting so drunk that she doesn't remember running into the same exec (in disguise) from her "meeting" and wakes up, naked, next to his godlike, nude form. C. Repeating all of B the VERY NEXT NIGHT except for waking up naked next to the dude (still saw him, though); D. Gets drunk her first night in Italy...AGAIN... 
 Why is she in Italy, you ask? Well, she goes to work on day two...three hours late...to find out that exec has offered her a job. And her boss fires her to make her take it. So she goes to the new building (don't even get me started on her driving her car in NYC), and the model-beautiful receptionist knows who she is, gives her a contract, benefit package, smartphone (I'm assuming, it never says how she gets it), and tickets to Italy for the following day. Dumbass takes it all in awe, never bothering to ask what the job is. Or wonder why she's hired. Or if she's qualified. Or why she isn't starting work immediately. 
 What's a girl to do? Go get wasted of course (but really, she doesn't drink. Seriously). Fast forward to Italy: exec reveals his identity (leaving it up to the intrepid reader to realize that he's actually Christian Grey...a pale, pale, shadow, but definitely there). Sexual tension abounds. Cue sex contract. Exec is also trying to purchase neighboring 800 acres of Italian waterfront to dice up into Hollywood getaways. Said property is owned by dying man with no heirs. Except our drunken heroine is mysteriously receiving foreign correspondence, according to the drunken whore roommate. I didn't read enough to find out if she winds up being the heir, but I would bet my left toenail she is. 
 Readers now endure endless sexual tension, brooding looks from the exec hinting at an unhappy childhood, and more vapid stupidity from the heroine. Who barely works. They finally bone, and watching paint dry is more entertaining. I tried to give it one final chance so I could finish the book until dummy wakes up alone in exec's bed, and this line happens: 
 "...As I lay on my back, staring at my reflection in the oversized mirror above my head, I could see something in my eyes that hadn't been there before." Aside from the whole 80s mirror above the bed thing, let's be real: you can't see details. Especially not an expression in your own eyeballs. I have to get up close and personal just to pluck my eyebrows, and I had LASIK.

sample_reviews.review_text: I really enjoyed Shadow of the Wind, so I was really looking forward to reading this. This is beautifully written with enough plot twists and interesting/amusing dialogues to keep you whipping through this long book to find out what happens next. My only criticisms would be about the character of Christine - I could why she would fall in love with David, but aside from being told how beautiful she was, we're not really given enough information about her to see why he would be so crazy about her: and then there's Corelli, who's never really explained. Supposedly all is explained in the third novel of the Barcelona trilogy, so I guess I will have to pick that one up. Still, this is probably the best book I've read in the last 6-12 months.
What a shock to discover that this book was tedious and uninspiring. So disappointing since I think his book "The Shadow of the Wind" was brilliant.

I really wanted to like this book. It was my first Zafon novel and I had high hopes based on all of the critical praise for his writings. 
 Generally I found The Angel's Game to be a mess of a book. There are plots and sub-plots wound around one another for us to untie, which is fine but I don't think our guide allowed us enough rope to do the job well and he left us hanging in many areas. Zafon also wrote "...these are just stories that share a universe, a tone and some central themes and characters. You don't need to care or know about any of this stuff to enjoy them." My question then is, if we "don't need to care or know about any of this stuff", what is the point? I read to become a part of a world I care about with characters that have meaning to me during the time I am reading about them. I was engaged with The Angel's Game, but after each chapter I kept thinking :"Maybe the big stuff starts in the next chapter". My whole read was one of anticipation that never became fulfilled. 
 A novel about a writer, books and language has a wonderful appeal to me so that aspect of the book was appreciated. The overall theme of good and evil always has potential as do the intricacies of human nature. At the end of the story I just felt lament for what could have been. I have been given a better sense of what to expect from The Shadow of the Wind, which I own, and I expect it will be a more pleasurable read than this first date with Zafon.

The writting style is just as good as many other titles of the same author. The story , though was not as impressive as, for instance, "La Sombra del Viento". To my mind, some aspects or details remain unexplained or the explanations are just incomplete. It was not as clear as many other Zafon's stories, but still enjoyed it.

Like me, you will probably read The Angels' Game because you enjoyed immensely the author's The Shadow of the Wind. And it's all here again: the musty dusty bookstores of Barcelona with their Borges-like labyrinths and secret passageways. Decaying old mansions; a brooding half-crazed, over-caffeinated writer; darkness, shadows, death, murders, mystery and foreboding. The problem I had was with the plot. I couldn't tell at the end what the resolution was of the plot. I even skimmed back though the book trying to see what I must have missed and if I could figure it out - no luck. It's still a good read; just not as good as Shadow.
I enjoyed reading this, but I didn't like it nearly as much as "Shadow the the Wind." I just didn't find it as dark or suspenseful as I felt it was trying to be.
Predictable, therefore disappointing.

This book reminds me a lot of the TV show "LOST". If you were a sucker like me, you tuned in like clockwork for 5 years and watched a lot of random unexplained crap that the producers assured us would be fully explained in good time. As soon as the last second of the finale aired without a single promised explanation, we all thought "Well, they lied" (or at least they did at the special event screening I watched it at. Seriously, there were 300 of us with WTF faces). 
 I digress. 
 Anyway, the book takes place a few decades prior to the events in The Shadow of the Wind. Aside from a few encounters with Daniel's grandfather and a few trips to the Cemetery of Forgotten Books, there's little to truly enjoy. 
 Instead, this book has all of the ennui and misery with none of the fun. Carlos Zafon has a thing for creepy old houses and intentionally miserable people. The protagonist of this book is David Martin, a penny dreadful writer with no family, few friends, and a hopeless crush on a mopey nutcase named Cristina. He chooses to live in a drafty, scary old house. Now if I moved into an old house and found a bunch of cool stuff the previous owners left behind and a freaking SECRET PASSAGEWAY! the first thing I'd do is grab my flashlight and holy water and start exploring. Instead, David just goes "meh" and ignores it. 
 His luck changes - sort of - when a mysterious man offers him a lucrative writing contract. Weird stuff starts to happen. There is also an encounter with a ghost prostitute. You know, if that happened to me, I'd start looking for answers or check myself into the funny farm. Nope, our boy David just shrugs it off. His only joy in life is the delightful Isabella, a teenager who moves in with 30 year old David to become his personal assistant. In early 1900s Spain. Yeah. Totally plausible, right? 
 The novel is a slow burn and takes its sweet time getting to the action. It wasn't until the last 100 pages or so that I realized most of the action takes place in the course of a few months, but felt like it took years. I tore through the last pages excitedly and was extremely disappointed with the "LOST"-esque resolution (which makes complete lack thereof). 
 I did enjoy the ride, though. I'm really torn with the rating. It's a perfect 2.5. 2 because it ultimately sucked and was a waste of time, but it was a lot of fun getting there. Ah well, 2 it is.

sample_reviews.review_text:
My first experience with a Gaiman novel and I'm still trying to sort through it in my head. I did really enjoy the story, and the story telling style he has. I'll definitely be reading more of his works, when I want something a bit more challenging and emotional than my usual escapist fare. 
 All the feels are present in this book and at the end I found myself with more questions than answers. But I suppose that was the point of the story all along, and in that it succeeded mightily. I was uncomfortable with the narrative for a short bit (child endangerment trigger) but thankfully that part was short lived, even if the resolution (erasing the incident as though it never happened) left me uncomfortable as well.

2.5 stars. Do you ever read a book that's good, on a technical level, but which you kind of hate anyway? I feel like that's what just happened to me. 
 You know what the problem is? I knew all the themes and the places this book would go. Do you know how I knew everything? Because it's the exact same themes as The Graveyard Book. And Coraline. And probably some of his other books too. It's about letting go of your childhood. Which is cool. It's a good theme. But I can't read an entire book with no other appeal. 
 I can acknowledge Gaiman is a great author. His imagery is pitch-perfect. Unfortunately, I don't know if that's really a good thing. If you've read this book, you know I'm talking body horror. The whole worm thing genuinely brought me one inch from DNFing this. Or dying, whichever came first. Don't read this if you're not a fan of body horror. Genuinely, do not. 
 The whole thing honestly just felt like a repeat of The Graveyard Book, but with less compelling characters. Yes, there were some nifty twists, but I somehow didn't care about any of it. This just felt so mediocre and angering to me, as a book. I felt like I should have loved it and I just didn't. 
 audiobook began: June 24th, 2017 
 Blog | Goodreads| Twitter | Youtube

This was my first book from Neil Gaiman (although I've watchedCoraline but as we all know, the movie may not be anything like the book, so I don't know if that's a true representation). I don't know what type of writing this is--I'd say a dark fairy tale? I'd give a 3.5 rounded down, it might be very good for its genre, but I don't read too many so I don't know. 
 It's a little disturbing to realize that we may have other lives being lived without our knowledge at any one time and that our world may just be a piece of canvas that covers something else. 
 The quote at the end of Saving Private Ryan--"earn it"--is very similar to the ending here, but I thought it was very realistic when the boy (Does he have a name? Even the cat has a name, Fluffy, but not the main character?) felt the weigh of the future guilt he might have. 
 I picked a hardcopy of this at a local bookstore, but the inside is stamped "no longer property of the Seattle public library"! Wonder how it got from Seattle to Northern Virginia!

Sometimes books come at just the right time. Another time, I might have been put off by the fanciful story in "The Ocean and the End of the Lane", but this week in November, days darkening and nostalgic, it was a tale in which I didn't mind getting lost.

The essential fairy tale has returned. 
 Great short book - set up is quick and efficient, no worries with all the background information on every character - it just dives right in. We are again brought back to the essential - the imaginative - the simple in order to tell and retell a story. Complete with heroes, heroines, evil doers, and a twist here and there. 
 I dare not go into details - what fun would that be? Go, and discover for yourself (and I bet you only need a day or two to in fact discover). Instead, I'll just leave with a few favorite quotes from the book - it gives a great snapshot of the tone of this little treasure. 
 "Adults follow paths. Children explore. Adults are content to walk the same way, hundreds of times, or thousands; perhaps it never occurs to adults to step off the paths, to creep beneath rhododendrons, to find the spaces between fences." 
 "Nobody actually looks like what they really are on the inside. You don't. People are much more complicated than that. It's true of everybody." 
 "When I left, I went with Lettie Hempstock and her mother out of the front door, and the moon was a thin white smile, high in a cloudy sky, and the night was gusty with sudden, undecided spring breezes coming first from one direction, then from another; every now and again a gust of wind would contain a sprinkling of rain that never amounted to anything more than that."

I have to be honest. I didn't like this book at all. I felt like I was duped based on the synopsis of the book. Although I appreciate that others liked it, I have to tell you that not one person liked it ... AT ALL. If it was going for fantasy, it missed and just became silly. One person in my BC said that they felt that it was written to become a movie. I think hey were probably right. But there's a reason why authors aren't screen writers! It's a different style completely. I'm glad that so many others liked it, but this was a major fail for me.

The opening chapter drew me in straight away and I settled into my armchair with a cup of tea and the anticipation of losing myself in the story - but sadly it just got too weird for me pretty quickly.

As someone who is only vaguely familiar with Gaiman's work, I have to say I wasn't overly impressed. An emotional story, but it sort of toes the genre line between adult and YA. I feel like the overarching plot is a tired one. It was a strange, short read. It was just okay for me. I didn't find his passages as profound as other readers seemed to. The book was too short to dig deep and resonate with me, but at the same time, I was so indifferent about the book that had it been much longer, I would have given up on it.

I feel like I missed the point of this book... I get some of the likely nuances, but otherwise, I definitely feel like I missed something. The story was definitely interesting, but again, I definitely feel like I'm missing something. However, I don't feel all that inclined to figure it out, which is unlike me, but I don't think I'm going to question it in this case... too many things to do and too many books left to read! Still, enjoyable book but not one I think I will be revisiting. 
 Note (added later 8/17/16): I feel the need to add that I've thought about this book for a little while now and I've come to a conclusion as for why I don't really care to dissect this book.... I found it somewhat depressing. The writing was terrific, as is the case with all of the writing I've read by Neil Gaiman, but ultimately this was not a book that made me feel all that good about myself and the world in the end. It was an interesting commentary on adulthood (yay! I think I figured out a little bit of the point of this book...), but ultimately it isn't something that I'm dying to reread or recommend. Still, if you are interested in a fantastical commentary on real life... this is the book for you.

Although I feel like I didn't completely understand this book, I was completely enchanted by it. It's been a while since I cringed or had nightmares about creatures from books, but that's what happened with this book. It was beautifully written, and I was so happy that Gaiman wrote this great addition to the genre of magical realism!

reference_books.title: The Autobiography of Henry VIII: With Notes by His Fool, Will Somers
reference_books.review_text:
An easy read and entertaining. But it adds nothing new. It is written from Henry VIII's (with occasional notes from his fool Will sommers) POV so it might pertain to the stereotypes. Yet they are too stereotypical for my like. The dowdy old sexy nun who may have lied, may not but it is too pretty and dumb and submissive and haughty and overbearing on poor young handsome Henry who is also irrritated by her disdain of English people and the Scots and repulsed by her "gift". Will adds that she is fat and while he criticizes Henry, he often excuses, lamenting that poor Henry was too much of a dreamer to see the evil oportunists, including his wives, who pulled his strings. Anne is the charming but evil conniving scheming witch who Summers constantly calls her as such, and Henry later describes as ugly and working her magic beyond the grave. Oh and Katherine of Aragon had the monstrous baby while Anne didn't (which historically there is no evidence that either gave birth to deformed babies, in regards to Anne, it was mostly later propaganda by enemies). Jane the demure passive wife. Anne of Cleves, the gigantic obese woman which makes Henry so repulsed. Catherine Howard -I almost breathed a sigh of relief that she wasn't depicted in the sa,e shade she's always depicted in fiction but that later went downhill with Will also calling her a slut and being so plain to everyone. The only wife who was portrayed accurtely (for the most part) was Katherine Parr. Her intelligence, wit, and charm, as well as her defense of her religion is well depicted here. 
 Lastly Henry's daughters fall into the same old categories, to quote Sommers here, Mary an ugly wench and angel of vengeance and to quote Henry VIII, Elizabeth is not beautiful enough but smarter and the new hope but too scheming to ever make anyone happy. Also, does the author know that the men Henry refers to as inexperienced youths who never had a taste of war (some of them) in fact were in a war before?! Edward Seymour was among the many knighted in the King's second battle with France. 
 The only courtier who was more or less assessed with good eyes by Henry and the author, was Thomas More. I felt the book was fairer to him than others. 
 And that leaves the rest of Henry's family. Henry VII the evil shadow, the specter, the miser who has no love for his wife, Elizabeth of York knows no happiness and yet she prefers Arthur over Henry, and then Meg Beaufort the evil old hag. 
 Great that she used the original letters (for that I gave it an extra star) but the portrayals were all stereotypical.

reference_books.title: Go Set a Watchman
reference_books.review_text:
There's been a lot of controversy regarding this book because of the character of Atticus Finch which was held as a paragon of virtue and justice. But reading this book, it makes to me perfect sense why he turned out the way he did and let me tell you why. Often times we think of racists as angry red-necks who just shout and spout terrible things. But we don't realize that racists can be the people we least expect. People who are considered so well-respected that you think 'no he or she can't be a racist' but it is their position of privilege, being so 'well-educated' that makes them apathetic to other people's plight. They are incredibly high and mighty elitists who feel they have no need for compassion. To me, that is Atticus Finch. As his daughter berates him towards the end of the book, the only reason he took the case in TKAM was because he felt he was doing his duty. He is all about 'duty' and 'honor'; he thinks himself better than anyone else. he says that what he is doing, and what he did TKAM, was to keep law and order because he is all about following the law. It makes me angry, because these types of racists are the most dangerous, because they are so well-respected, they are so charismatic and instead of defending themselves with angry words, they defend themselves with a smile and eloquence to confuse others. That is exactly what happened between Atticus and his daughter Jean-Louise. At the end **Spoilers** she is forced to accept the ugly truth and "welcome" her father "into the human race" and conform herself into the life -and the racist community- she was born. 
 A sad and (in my view) disappointing ending. Not because it is badly written, but because some people have to conform themselves to their parents' racist, religious fanatical, or other kind of bigoted ideals because of the love they have for them -and also because they are unable to come to grasp with the idea that their loved ones are like this, or (as I suspect in the case of Jean-Louise) because they are afraid of guilt. 
 I gave it three stars because of the disappointing ending and because it started off slow. But it has some really good parts that makes you feel angry, because these people still exist and it is so hard for them to open their eyes because like Atticus, they are so high and mighty, they can't see the harm of what they are doing to their fellow human beings. 
 What bugs me the most is that I grew up with a man that was similar to Atticus Finch. Yes, I have a dad like that -not exactly like that, but similar- and I still get in fights with him because he can't accept what I am: He can't accept that I am a feminist, that I am bisexual, that I stand for human rights, and most of all that I stand against misogyny. 
 As they say, sometimes the people that we love, turn out to be the worst.

reference_books.title: The Constant Princess (The Plantagenet and Tudor Novels, #6)
reference_books.review_text:
While I did not agree with some bits of Henry the seventh's portrayal on this book or her last ones; I liked her portrayal of Katherine of Aragon, more than in other historical fictions in fact. One of the reasons for this is that other books portray her as a woman incapable of lying, a woman who is the epitome of the good wife, the good Catholic wife who is ambitious but that ambition is not above her religion. 
 Katherine of Aragon was religious. Fact. Was Katherine of Aragon a woman incapable of lying, a woman who put God above all? There is no black and white answer for this. People may hate it or like it, but the truth is many actions (terrible or not) that people did during this time were done in accordance to their views of God. Many of the atrocities committed by her husband, her daughter, Elizabeth I, Edward VI, her nephew Charles I of Spain and V of the Holy Roman Empire, her grand-nephew Philip II of Spain were done with the point of view they are doing it in 'the name of god'. 
 These people saw themselves as pre-ordained to be kings, queens, princes, princesses, or rulers. Katherine might have never lied and her marriage to Arthur may have never been consummated; but it might also have been consummated and her belief that she was meant to be queen was so strong that she may have lied. To her it may not have been a lie. It might have been (like many kings and their armies that killed during the crusades, popes that swore on the name of god to uphold His law but did the opposite) excused under the belief that god was making her endure all these pains to prove herself worthy of being Queen. Katherine after all said during her last years that she preferred endurance over happiness because only then was she closer to god. 
 I am not saying everyone should agree for me, but it should give everyone food for thought. I don't agree with most of Gregory's portrayals but with Katherine she captured on her convictions and ambitions really well.
